Warm light from a rattan pendant shade and a small brass sconce. A white woman in her forties with curly hair sits on the sofa in a relaxed candid pose, feet tucked beneath her, a book in hand.]]

Bohemian reading room decor ideas by style variant

  • Natural boho: Raw linen, undyed cotton, dried botanicals, unglazed clay — earthy and calm
  • Modern boho: Clean furniture lines with boho textiles and plants layered on top — the most liveable option
  • Eclectic boho: Pattern on pattern, jewel colours, vintage finds — rich and maximalist, requires confident editing
  • Coastal boho: Natural rattan, driftwood, pampas grass, bleached linen — relaxed and breezy
  • Dark boho: Deep inky walls (forest green, charcoal, midnight blue) with warm natural textiles and abundant plants — dramatic and cosy
Pro Tip: The quickest route to a cohesive bohemian reading room (whatever the specific flavour) is to start with your textile — a rug you love — and pull your palette from that. If your rug has terracotta, sage and cream in it, let those three colours guide every other choice in the room.

More About Reading Corners and How to Get Them Right

A well-designed reading corner isn't a luxury — it's one of the most worthwhile small investments you can make in your everyday home life.

The research backs this up: dedicated reading spaces genuinely increase the amount people read, and reading itself has well-documented benefits for stress reduction, sleep quality, and mental wellbeing. It's worth getting the design right.

If you're looking for more visual inspiration and practical layout ideas beyond what I've covered here, the team at Living Etc have put together a thorough round-up of Reading corner ideas that's particularly strong on built-in and architectural solutions — worth a look if you're thinking about a more permanent setup.

What I'd add to any guide, and what I always come back to with clients, is this: the best reading corner isn't the one that looks most beautiful in a photo. It's the one you actually sit in every day. That means it has to be physically comfortable, well-lit, and in a spot in your home that you naturally gravitate to — not a tucked-away corner that's inconvenient to get to.

Start with those fundamentals. Build the atmosphere and the styling around them. And don't be afraid to move things around several times before you settle — the best reading corners usually take a few iterations to find their final form.

The most important thing I want you to take from all of this is that a great reading corner isn't about spending a lot or having a lot of space. It's about intention — choosing a spot, committing to it, and layering in the comfort and character that make it genuinely yours.

Your books deserve a good home. And so do you.

Hallway wall decor ideas can completely transform the first impression your home makes — and they don't have to cost a fortune or require a full renovation. Whether you've got a narrow Victorian corridor or a generous open entrance hall, the right combination of mirrors, artwork, shelves and colour can make it feel welcoming, stylish and genuinely you.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever walked into someone's hallway and immediately thought, "this house feels amazing" — before you've even seen the living room? That's the power of great wall art and thoughtful decor doing its job quietly in the background.

Quick answer: The best hallway wall decor ideas combine mirrors (to add light and depth), artwork or prints (to show personality), and functional elements like shelves or hooks. Tailor your choices to your hallway's size and light levels, and you'll create an entrance that sets the tone for your whole home.

Your hallway is literally the first room anyone sees, yet it's often the last one people decorate. A well-styled entrance uses unique wall art and unique home decor to create a cohesive mood that flows through the rest of the house. Think of it as your home's handshake — it should feel confident, warm and entirely intentional.

Types of Hallway Wall Decor Ideas (Gallery Walls, Mirrors, Artwork, Shelves)

When it comes to hallway wall decor ideas, there are four main categories worth knowing: gallery walls, mirrors, standalone artwork, and wall-mounted shelves. Each does something different for the space, and the best hallways often layer two or three together.

Gallery walls work brilliantly in hallways because they draw the eye along the corridor, making the walk feel intentional rather than just functional. Mirrors open up the space visually, artwork gives personality, and shelves let you bring in texture through plants, ceramics and books.

Pro Tip: If you're unsure where to start, pick just ONE type of decor for your hallway first — a mirror or a shelf — and live with it for a couple of weeks before adding more. It's much easier to build up than to edit back.

Choosing the Right Style for Your Hallway

The style you choose for your hallway should reflect the broader feel of your home — not clash with it the moment guests step inside. That said, your hallway can absolutely be a little bolder than other rooms because people pass through it quickly.

Modern hallways suit clean lines, monochrome palettes and graphic prints. Traditional homes often call for warmer tones, ornate mirrors and botanical artwork. Minimalist spaces work beautifully with a single oversized piece, negative space and nothing unnecessary on the walls.

Matching Style to Your Home

  • Modern / contemporary: Go for abstract prints, clean geometric mirrors, monochrome or muted palettes. Keep accessories to a minimum.
  • Traditional / period home: Warm heritage colours, ornate gilt or dark-wood frames, botanical or landscape artwork, classic console table beneath.
  • Minimalist: One strong hero piece of wall art, a single sculptural object, nothing cluttered. Let the wall breathe.
  • Eclectic / maximalist: Mix frame styles intentionally, layer textures, include a macramé hanging or woven wall piece alongside prints.
  • Coastal / natural: Sandy tones, natural rattan or woven wall hangings, botanical and seascape prints, driftwood or ceramic wall hooks.
Pro Tip: The mistake I always see is people decorating their hallway in a completely different style to the rest of the house. It creates a jarring moment every time you walk through the door. Take one or two key colours from your living room and echo them in your hallway decor — it creates flow without being matchy-matchy.

Paint and Colour Ideas for Hallway Walls

Paint is arguably the most powerful tool you have in a hallway — and it costs less than any piece of furniture. The right colour can make a narrow corridor feel wider, a dark hallway feel brighter, and a plain space feel rich and considered.

Pale, warm whites and soft off-whites (think warm cream rather than bright white) work in almost every hallway. If you want drama, a deep tone on the lower half — separated by a dado rail — is a classic British trick that grounds the space without making it feel oppressive.

Colour Choices and What They Do

  • Warm white / soft cream: Reflects light, feels welcoming, works with almost any decor style.
  • Sage green: Calm, nature-inspired, pairs beautifully with natural wood and rattan decor.
  • Deep charcoal or navy: Dramatic and sophisticated — works best in hallways with overhead lighting or a window.
  • Warm terracotta or blush: Creates an inviting, cosy tone; works brilliantly with brass or gold accents.
  • Two-tone (dado rail split): Classic British technique — deeper tone below, lighter above — adds architectural interest to any hallway.
  • Limewash / textured paint effect: Adds visual depth without additional decor — very on-trend in natural interior styles right now.
Real Example: A client of mine had a north-facing hallway that felt freezing cold in tone — she'd painted it a stark bright white. We switched to a warm sandy off-white with a dusky pink-blush dado below, added two small brass wall sconces, and the hallway suddenly felt like it was glowing even on the dreariest January morning.

How to Arrange Wall Decor in a Narrow Hallway

Narrow hallways are one of the most common challenges I hear about, and the good news is they're very solvable. The key is to work vertically rather than horizontally — draw the eye up, not across, and you'll feel more space immediately.

Keep everything flush to the wall to protect the walkway. Avoid anything that protrudes more than a few centimetres — no bulky frames, no oversized brackets. A slim floating shelf at chest height or a flat mirror are your best friends here.

Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Narrow Hallway Arrangement Tips

  • Hang artwork in a vertical column rather than a horizontal row — this draws the eye upward and makes ceilings feel higher.
  • Use one large mirror instead of multiple small ones — it'll do more work for the space.
  • Choose slim-profile floating shelves no deeper than 15–20cm so they don't eat into the walkway.
  • Use wall sconces (wall-mounted lights) instead of a floor lamp — they free up floor space entirely.
  • Avoid gallery walls on BOTH walls opposite each other in a very narrow hall — stick to one feature wall.
  • A runner rug down the centre draws the eye along the corridor and adds warmth without taking any wall space.
Pro Tip: For a narrow hallway, hang your main mirror at eye level — roughly 145–155cm from the floor to its centre. Any higher and it stops doing its job of bouncing light; any lower and it feels like a bathroom vanity mirror rather than a hallway statement piece.

What is the Best Artwork to Hang in a Hallway?

The best artwork to hang in a hallway is whatever you genuinely love to see every single day — but practically speaking, there are a few formats and subjects that work particularly well in this high-traffic, often narrow space.

Vertically oriented prints and paintings work better than wide horizontal pieces in most hallways. Subject matter that's calming and welcoming — botanicals, landscapes, abstract shapes, simple line art — tends to work better than anything busy or jarring right at the entrance to your home.

Best Artwork Formats for Hallways

  • Tall portrait prints (A2, A1 or 50x70cm): Ideal for single-piece statements in narrow or medium-width hallways.
  • Triptych sets (three matching prints): Hung in a vertical column or a tight horizontal trio, these feel collected and curated.
  • Botanical line art: Clean, simple, works in both modern and traditional homes.
  • Abstract prints in earthy tones: Calming rather than stimulating — exactly right for an entrance space.
  • Photography prints: Family photographs or landscape photography add personality without being overly decorative.
  • Minimal typography prints: A single meaningful word or phrase — works best in modern or Scandi-style hallways.
Pro Tip: Hang your main piece of hallway artwork so its centre sits at approximately 145–150cm from the floor — that's the standard "eye level" hang height used by most gallery curators, and it works in almost every home.

What is Japandi Wall Art?

Japandi is the design style that combines Japanese minimalism with Scandinavian warmth — and it has become one of the most popular interior aesthetics in the UK for good reason. Japandi wall art follows those same principles: understated, calm, natural, and deeply intentional.

Typically, Japandi wall art features minimal compositions — think a single brushstroke, a sparse branch, a clean abstract shape, or a neutral-toned nature study. The colour palette stays within quiet earth tones: warm whites, soft beige, ash grey, charcoal, terracotta and forest green.

Key Characteristics of Japandi Wall Art

  • Minimal compositions with significant negative space — "breathing room" around the subject is intentional.
  • Nature-inspired subjects: branches, pebbles, water, leaves, bamboo, foliage, or abstract organic shapes.
  • Muted, natural colour palettes — warm neutrals, dusty greens, charcoal, ash, soft terracotta.
  • Handmade or hand-drawn quality — brushstroke art, lino prints, woodblock-inspired prints are very on-brand.
  • Simple, unobtrusive frames — natural wood, bamboo, thin black metal or even frameless mounting suits it perfectly.
Pro Tip: The mistake people make with Japandi wall art is hanging too many pieces. One or two prints in this style, with space between them, will always outperform a crowded gallery wall. Restraint is literally part of the design philosophy.

Japandi Hallway Wall Art Ideas

Japandi hallway wall art ideas are perfect for the entrance space because the style's core values — calm, simplicity, natural warmth — are exactly what you want guests to feel the moment they walk in. It also works brilliantly in narrow hallways because the minimal aesthetic never feels cluttered.

Some of my favourite Japandi hallway wall art ideas include a single large branch or botanical print in a thin natural wood frame, a set of two or three small circular woven wall hangings grouped asymmetrically, or a simple abstract brushstroke print in charcoal on a warm white background.

Japandi Hallway Wall Art Ideas to Try

  • Single oversized botanical sprig or branch print in a slim natural frame — classic and always works.
  • A grouping of two or three small circular woven wall hangings in natural cotton or jute.
  • Abstract brushstroke print in charcoal, ash or warm terracotta — large format for maximum impact.
  • Minimalist line-drawing of a mountain, wave, or forest in a frameless or thin black frame.
  • A wabi-sabi inspired textured ceramic wall panel or plaque — adds three-dimensional interest.
  • Japanese kanji or Nordic rune-inspired typographic print — single word, clean, calm.
Real Example: I styled a narrow Victorian hallway for a client who had fallen in love with Japandi style but couldn't understand why her hallway felt "off." She'd hung five small prints in different sizes. We replaced them with one single A1 brushstroke print in a warm ash frame and placed a woven wall hanging beside the door hook. The whole hallway exhaled. That's Japandi working properly.

Large Japandi Hallway Wall Art: When to Go Big

Large Japandi hallway wall art is one of the most impactful choices you can make for a medium or generous-sized entrance. A single large piece — think A1 (59x84cm) or even 70x100cm — anchors the space and immediately gives it a gallery-like calm.

The beauty of going large in the Japandi style is that the minimal composition means it never overwhelms. A single large branch on a warm white background has enormous presence without being visually noisy. That's the whole point.

Sizing Guide for Large Japandi Hallway Wall Art

  • Small hallway (under 1m wide): Maximum A2 (42x59cm) for a single print — go larger and it'll dominate too much.
  • Medium hallway (1–1.5m wide): A1 (59x84cm) is ideal — large enough to anchor, not so large it overwhelms.
  • Generous hallway (over 1.5m wide): 70x100cm or even a diptych (two panels together) works beautifully.
  • Always leave at least 15–20cm of wall visible above the print and to both sides — the breathing space is part of the Japandi aesthetic.
  • Hang the centre of a large print at 145–150cm from the floor, regardless of ceiling height.
Pro Tip: With large Japandi wall art, resist the urge to add more pieces around it. Let it stand alone. Add interest through texture at a different level — a shelf beneath, a woven rug below — rather than competing with the artwork at eye level.

Modern Japandi Hallway Home Decor

Modern Japandi hallway home decor takes the core philosophy of Japandi — calm, natural materials, intentional simplicity — and gives it a slightly more contemporary, less rustic edge. Think clean architectural lines, matte black metal accents, and a tighter, more curated edit.

In practice, modern Japandi hallway home decor often means a slim, low-profile console table in pale oak with black metal legs, a single architectural wall sconce in matte black, and one carefully chosen piece of wall art. No clutter. No excess.

Modern Japandi Hallway Decor Essentials

  • Slim console table: pale oak or ash wood with black or bronze metal legs — keep it under 30cm deep.
  • Wall sconce in matte black or aged brass — functional and architectural, freeing up the floor.
  • Circular mirror with a thin metal or natural wood frame at eye level.
  • One ceramic object on the shelf — sculptural, matte finish, earth tone.
  • A single trailing plant or dried pampas stems in a tall, simple vase.
  • A natural fibre runner rug (jute or sisal) in a plain weave — no busy patterns.
Pro Tip: In a modern Japandi hallway, every object should earn its place. Before adding anything new, ask: does this serve a purpose, or do I genuinely find it beautiful? If neither, it shouldn't be there.

If you do nothing else, try this: clear everything off your hallway wall, remove anything that isn't useful or beautiful, then add just one natural-material piece — a woven wall hanging, a ceramic hook rack, a trailing plant on a slim shelf. See how the space immediately breathes.

Quick Japandi Hallway Decor Changes for This Weekend

  • Swap any plastic or synthetic hooks for a simple ceramic or natural wood hook rail.
  • Add a small propagation vase with a trailing plant cutting to your hallway shelf — it costs almost nothing.
  • Replace a cluttered pinboard or corkboard with a single woven macramé wall hanging.

  • Invest in one good quality natural fibre rug (jute, sisal, seagrass) to replace a synthetic mat.
  • Switch to a warm-tone bulb in your hallway light fitting — it instantly changes the mood without touching a wall.
Pro Tip: You don't need to spend anything to make your hallway feel more Japandi this weekend. Start by removing rather than adding — take out everything that's synthetic, plastic, or brightly coloured, and see what's left. That's your Japandi starting point.

Small Hallway vs Large Hallway Decor Strategies

The strategy for a small hallway is completely different to what works in a large one — and many people make the mistake of using the same approach for both. Getting this right makes an enormous difference.

In a small hallway, every piece of decor must work harder. You simply don't have the luxury of a decorative object that doesn't also serve a function. In a large hallway, the challenge flips — you need enough pieces to fill the space without it feeling empty or echoey.

[[IMG|small-vs-large-hallway-decor-strategy|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Small Hallway vs Large Hallway: Decor Strategy". Then a clear VISUAL comparison: two labelled side-by-side hallway illustrations — left side labelled "Small Hallway" with callout labels showing: tall mirror, one slim shelf, vertical art, wall sconce — right side labelled "Large Hallway" with callout labels showing: gallery wall, console table with lamp, large area rug, multiple light sources, statement mirror. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Strategy by Hallway Size

  • Small hallways: One mirror (tall, slim), one slim shelf, wall-mounted hooks (not freestanding coat rack), vertical artwork only, wall sconce instead of floor lamp.
  • Medium hallways: Can support a gallery wall on one side, a console table, a standing mirror or wall mirror, a small rug.
  • Large hallways: Think in zones — an arrival zone near the door, a display zone further in. Use larger artwork, a statement mirror, potentially a bench or chair, a generous rug.
  • In large hallways, overhead lighting alone often isn't enough — layer with wall sconces or table lamp on console.
  • In small hallways, avoid anything that reduces floor or walkway space — freestanding items are almost always a mistake.
Real Example: I visited a client with a wide, airy entrance hall who had filled it with tiny prints and small objects — it looked like a gift shop. We replaced everything with two large-scale pieces: a substantial round mirror and one generous abstract print in a warm ash frame, plus a wide console table and a proper area rug. The hall finally felt like it matched the size of the house.

How to Make a Dark Hallway Feel Brighter with Wall Decor

A dark hallway is one of the most common problems in UK homes — especially in terraced houses and flats where the entrance gets no natural light at all. Wall decor is one of your most effective tools for fixing this, often more impactful than changing the light fitting itself.

Mirrors are the obvious starting point, but it's not just about adding one mirror — it's about placing it to actively reflect whatever light exists, whether that's from an open door, a staircase window, or a light fitting. Position the mirror directly opposite or at an angle to the light source.

[[IMG|dark-hallway-brighter-wall-decor-tips|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A north-facing UK hallway that has been brightened through wall decor: a large oval mirror with a slim natural rattan frame sits prominently on the main wall, reflecting light from an open doorway at the end. Two warm-glow wall sconces flank the mirror on either side. A slim shelf below holds a small pot of real trailing ivy and a cream ceramic vase. Walls in warm soft white. A mixed-heritage woman in her late 30s is walking through the hallway, smiling, in a relaxed natural candid motion. The space feels warm and inviting despite having no windows directly in view.]]

Wall Decor Tricks for Dark Hallways

  • Place a large mirror directly opposite your front door — it bounces any incoming natural light back into the hall.
  • Use wall sconces with warm-white bulbs (2700–3000K) rather than cool overhead lighting — it feels warmer and more welcoming.
  • Choose wall art in lighter tones — pale botanical prints, light abstract washes — rather than dark-toned artwork.
  • Use a gloss or semi-gloss finish on the wall paint rather than flat matt — it reflects more light subtly.
  • Install a small internal glass panel or fanlight above the door if possible — brings light from outside without structural work.
  • Add a trailing plant on a shelf — green living plants reflect light and add life to a dark space.
Pro Tip: The most budget-friendly bright hallway trick I know: paint the ceiling the same warm white as the walls (not brilliant white — warm white). Most people paint ceilings brilliant white as default, but in a dark hallway that cool tone makes the ceiling feel even more distant and cold. Warm white throughout is transformative.
[[PRODUCT|wall sconce hallway lighting brass warm glow]]

Budget-Friendly vs Premium Hallway Wall Decor Options

You genuinely don't need to spend a lot to create a beautiful hallway — but knowing where to invest and where to save is the key. I always tell clients: spend on the one or two pieces that will anchor the room (the mirror, the main artwork), and save everywhere else.

Budget options can look just as good as expensive ones if you're thoughtful about quality and placement. A single well-chosen print in a frame you've found second-hand will always look better than ten cheap items crammed together.

[[IMG|budget-vs-premium-hallway-wall-decor|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Budget vs Premium: Where to Spend in Your Hallway". Then a clear VISUAL comparison: two labelled columns — left column labelled "Save" with simple icons for: DIY gallery wall, second-hand frames, printed art downloads, jute rug, trailing plant — right column labelled "Invest" with icons for: statement mirror, quality artwork print, wall sconces, slim console table. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Where to Save and Where to Spend

  • Spend on: A good quality mirror (the frame matters — cheap frames look cheap), one statement print or artwork, wall-mounted lighting.
  • Save on: Gallery wall filler prints (use black-and-white photo prints from home), frames (charity shops and car boot sales are gold), decorative objects on shelves.
  • DIY wins: Paint a single wall an accent colour yourself — costs under £30 and transforms the space. Create a simple macramé wall hanging from YouTube tutorials — natural cotton rope costs very little.
  • Avoid false economy: Cheap sticky picture hooks that damage walls, very lightweight frames that warp, synthetic materials that look plasticky up close.
Pro Tip: If budget is tight, buy one genuinely good print and display it in a simple, slim frame rather than buying three average prints. One piece of wall art you love will make a better impression — and make you happier every day — than a collection of things you settled for.

Seasonal and Easily Swappable Hallway Wall Decor Ideas

Your hallway is actually the perfect place for seasonal decor changes because it's small enough that swapping things out doesn't take long, and it immediately refreshes the whole feel of your home. I love this approach — it means your entrance always feels current and considered.

The trick is to build a base of permanent pieces (mirror, shelf, hooks) and then swap the small seasonal layer on top: a print, a vase of seasonal flowers or branches, a wreath, a different coloured runner rug.

[[IMG|seasonal-swappable-hallway-wall-decor|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A hallway shelf styled for autumn: a ceramic vase holds dried orange and rust-toned honesty seed pods and dried hydrangea heads. A small woven wall hanging in warm amber and terracotta tones hangs above the shelf. A round mirror with a natural rattan frame reflects the warm-toned display. The floor has a rust-toned natural wool runner. A South Asian woman in her 50s and her teenage daughter are arranging dried stems in the vase together, laughing, in a warm natural candid moment. Rich warm afternoon light, ochre-toned walls.]]

Seasonal Swaps by Time of Year

  • Spring: Fresh green trailing plants on the shelf, botanical print in soft greens and whites, a light linen runner rug.
  • Summer: Coastal or floral print, a jute or seagrass rug, dried lavender bundles tied with twine as a natural wall hanging.
  • Autumn: Dried seed pods or honesty stems in a vase, a warm amber or terracotta toned wall hanging, a wool runner in rust or ochre.
  • Winter: A eucalyptus wreath on the door (or the wall), dried orange slice garland on a shelf, a print with cool silver or navy tones.
  • Year-round base pieces: Mirror, hook rail, slim shelf, wall sconce — these stay constant; everything else can rotate.
Pro Tip: Keep a small box or basket in a cupboard with your off-season hallway pieces — a couple of prints, a small seasonal vase, a folded runner. Swapping them takes ten minutes and costs nothing once you've built up a small collection over time.

Specific Product Recommendations with Sizing Guidance for Hallways

One of the biggest frustrations I hear from people decorating their hallways is buying something online only to find it's the completely wrong scale when it arrives. So here's the practical sizing guidance I always give my clients — before they buy a thing.

The hallway is unforgiving with sizing mistakes because the space is small and you see it every day at close range. Getting the proportions right matters more here than in any other room.

[[IMG|hallway-decor-product-sizing-guidance|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A well-organised UK hallway with clearly sized decor elements: a tall oval mirror at eye level, a slim pale oak shelf with a ceramic vase and small trailing plant, a natural cotton macramé wall hanging above. The space is uncluttered and proportional. A white British man in his 40s is measuring the wall with a tape measure in a practical, focused candid manner, preparing to hang something. Warm neutral walls, pale oak parquet floor. Natural soft daylight.]]

Sizing Cheat Sheet for Hallway Decor

  • Wall art — small hallway: Maximum A2 (42x59cm) portrait orientation. Any bigger and it'll overwhelm the space.
  • Wall art — medium hallway: A1 (59x84cm) is ideal. For a diptych, two A2s side by side works well.
  • Wall art — large hallway: Up to 70x100cm for a single piece. Consider a triptych or diptych for a gallery feel.
  • Mirror: At least 60cm tall for a hallway mirror to do its job properly. Full-length (at least 120cm) if space allows.
  • Shelf depth: Maximum 20cm in a narrow hall; 25–30cm is fine in a medium or generous hall.
  • Console table: No deeper than 30cm — ideally 25cm in a narrow hallway. Height around 75–80cm is standard.
  • Runner rug: Should cover roughly 80% of the hallway floor length; leave 15–20cm of floor visible at each end.
Pro Tip: Before buying anything for your hallway, cut out newspaper or brown parcel paper to the exact size of the piece you're considering and tape it to the wall. Live with it for a day. You'll know immediately whether the scale is right — and you'll save yourself a return trip.
[[PRODUCT|abstract wall art prints large format hallway]] [[PRODUCT|ceramic wall hooks hallway decor]]

Hallway Wall Decor Styles Worth Bookmarking

If you're looking for visual inspiration beyond the basics, here's a roundup of the hallway aesthetics that are genuinely doing well in real homes right now — and what makes each one work.

Visual Inspiration

Explore complementary design ideas on our Home Decor by Trend page:

  • Modern Contemporary Home Decor Trend - sleek stylish hallway wall inspiration
  • Cosy Minimalism Home Decor Trend - calm understated hallway decor ideas
  • Eclectic Maximalist Home Decor Trend - bold layered hallway wall displays

More About Styling Your Hallway Well

Your hallway does more emotional work than almost any other room in your home — it sets the mood for everything that follows.

Getting it right is a combination of understanding your space's physical constraints (narrow, dark, low-ceilinged), choosing a style that connects to the rest of your home, and then being disciplined about not overcrowding it. If you want a broader look at current hallway decor thinking, the team at Velux have put together a genuinely useful overview of approaches — take a look at 10 Hallway decor ideas to really make an entrance for a complementary perspective, particularly on how light plays into the whole picture.

The most important thing I'd tell anyone styling their hallway: be more considered, not more filled. The hallways I've seen that feel genuinely beautiful are almost always the ones where someone had the confidence to put less on the walls, not more.

WATCH: Top 100 Hallway Decor Ideas 2023 - Narrow Hallway Interior Design - Modern Wall Home Decor Ideas

Ready to Start Your Hallway Transformation?

I hope this guide has given you a genuinely useful starting point — not just inspiration, but actual practical decisions you can make today about what to put on your hallway walls and how to place it.

Remember: your hallway doesn't need to be perfect, it just needs to feel like you. Whether that's a Japandi-calm entrance with one carefully chosen brushstroke print and a woven wall hanging, or a warm maximalist gallery wall covered in family photographs and botanical prints — if it makes you smile when you walk through the door, it's doing its job.

So tell me — what does your hallway look like right now, and what's the one thing you'd most like to change about it?
hallway wall decor ideas.heroPrompt: A wide, beautifully styled UK hallway entrance. The main wall features a slim pale ash floating shelf holding a tall ceramic bud vase with dried pampas stems and a small trailing pothos plant, with a large oval mirror in a natural rattan frame mounted above at eye level. Two warm-glow brass wall sconces flank the mirror symmetrically. A thin-profile ceramic hook rail is mounted beside the door. The floor has a natural jute runner rug with a simple bordered edge. Walls in warm limewash plaster in a soft greige tone. A pale oak console table with black metal hairpin legs stands below the shelf. The space feels calm, warm, edited and lived-in — Japandi-influenced but with British character. Soft diffused natural light from an open front door at the far end of the hall. No framed pictures or prints on the walls.

farmhouse kitchen ideas.bodyHtml:
Farmhouse kitchen ideas are having a real moment right now, and honestly, it's easy to see why — that warm, lived-in, slightly rustic look just makes a kitchen feel like the heart of the home. Whether you're starting from scratch or trying to refresh what you've already got, there's so much you can do beyond swapping out cabinet handles. In this guide, I'm going to walk you through every layer of the farmhouse kitchen look, from flooring to wall art to lighting, so you can build a space that actually feels like yours.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever walked into someone's kitchen and just thought, "I want to live here"? That feeling almost always comes down to the details — the textures, the colours, the little touches on the walls. It's exactly why I think wall art and decorative styling are the most underrated tools in any kitchen makeover. Most people focus on the big-ticket items and then wonder why the space still feels a bit flat.

Quick answer: The best farmhouse kitchen ideas combine natural materials, muted earthy tones, and warm lighting with carefully chosen wall art, prints, and styling accessories. You don't need to gut your kitchen — targeted changes to walls, furniture, and decor can completely shift the feel of the space.

Farmhouse style in the kitchen is all about warmth, practicality, and a sense that the room has been lived in and loved over time. It draws on traditional country aesthetics — think shiplap, butler sinks, open shelving, and natural wood — but it doesn't have to feel dated or heavy. If you're looking for unique wall art that fits a farmhouse kitchen or some unique home decor to pull the whole look together, I've got you covered throughout this guide.

List of Contents

  • Farmhouse Kitchen Cabinet and Color Ideas
  • Farmhouse Kitchen Decor and Wall Art
  • Farmhouse Kitchen Furniture and Layout
  • Farmhouse Kitchen Lighting Ideas
  • Farmhouse Kitchen Flooring and Backsplash
  • Wall Art and Printable Decor Specifically Styled for Farmhouse Kitchens
  • DIY and Budget-Friendly Farmhouse Kitchen Makeover Tips
  • How to Mix Modern and Rustic Farmhouse Elements
  • Seasonal and Functional Farmhouse Kitchen Styling
  • Farmhouse Kitchen Decor Shopping Guide with Product Recommendations
  • How to Decorate a Kitchen Wall Farmhouse Style
  • Modern Farmhouse Kitchen Wall Art
  • Rustic Farmhouse Kitchen Wall Art
  • Farmhouse Kitchen Home Decor Ideas
  • Modern Farmhouse Kitchen Home Decor
  • Rustic Farmhouse Kitchen Home Decor
  • Farmhouse Kitchen and Living Room Decor
  • Farmhouse Kitchen Styles and Looks to Inspire You
  • More About Farmhouse Kitchens
  • Let's Keep the Conversation Going

Farmhouse Kitchen Cabinet and Color Ideas

Your cabinets and colour palette are the foundation of the whole farmhouse kitchen look, so it's worth getting these right before anything else. The good news is you have a lot of options, whether you're painting existing units or starting fresh.

Classic farmhouse cabinet colours sit firmly in the muted, earthy camp — think off-white, warm cream, sage green, dusty blue, or soft taupe. These shades work because they don't fight with the natural materials (wood, stone, linen) that the style relies on. I generally steer clients away from stark white because it reads as modern rather than farmhouse.

[[IMG|farmhouse-kitchen-cabinet-color-ideas|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling unless this section is about another interior style. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A warm, inviting farmhouse kitchen with shaker-style cabinets painted in a muted sage green on the lower units and off-white on the upper units, natural wood open shelving above displaying simple ceramic crockery and small potted herbs, a cream-toned stone worktop, and a Belfast sink with aged brass taps. Warm light streams through a small window above the sink. A Black British woman in her mid-thirties stands at the sink washing vegetables in a relaxed candid pose, wearing a soft linen apron.]]

Cabinet and Colour Quick Guide

  • Shaker-style doors — the most versatile cabinet style for farmhouse; works in both rustic and modern versions
  • Off-white or cream — timeless and pairs beautifully with warm wood accents
  • Sage green — popular right now and reads as both modern and traditionally farmhouse
  • Dusty navy — a bolder option for lower cabinets that adds depth without going dark
  • Open shelving — replace a few upper cabinet doors with open shelves to display ceramics and jars
  • Mixed finishes — two-tone cabinets (different uppers and lowers) add character
  • Hardware — brushed brass, black iron, or aged bronze handles all suit the style

I once helped a client in Surrey who had a kitchen full of glossy white cabinets and couldn't understand why it felt clinical. We simply painted the lower units in a warm linen tone and replaced the chrome handles with black cast-iron bar pulls. The transformation cost very little but completely shifted the feeling of the room.

Pro Tip: If you're renting or on a tight budget, cabinet paint is your best friend. A good chalk-based paint in a heritage shade can completely change the character of your kitchen without a single structural change — and it's reversible.

Farmhouse Kitchen Decor and Wall Art

This is where I get really excited, because farmhouse kitchen decor is so much more than just a few enamel signs and a fruit bowl. The walls, the shelves, the surfaces — every inch is an opportunity to build warmth and personality into the space.

The mistake I always see is people decorating their entire kitchen and then leaving the walls completely bare. It's the equivalent of getting dressed and forgetting your shoes. The walls are what make a kitchen feel complete and cohesive.

[[IMG|farmhouse-kitchen-decor-wall-art|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling unless this section is about another interior style. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A cosy farmhouse kitchen dining area with a reclaimed wood shelf mounted on a cream-painted shiplap wall displaying small terracotta pots with trailing herbs, a woven macramé wall hanging, and a small oval mirror with a wooden frame. Below the shelf is a vintage-style enamel sign and a small wall-mounted lantern. A South Asian woman in her late twenties leans against the counter nearby, smiling, holding a mug of tea.]]

Farmhouse Kitchen Decor Must-Haves

  • Botanical or botanical-inspired prints in simple wooden or black frames
  • Typographic prints with kitchen phrases, herb names, or countryside motifs
  • Woven wall hangings or macramé in natural cotton or jute
  • Mounted wooden shelves displaying ceramics and trailing plants
  • Enamel or vintage-look signs used sparingly as a focal accent
  • Clocks with rustic metal or wooden frames
  • Small mirrors with distressed or natural wood frames to bounce light
[[PRODUCT|farmhouse kitchen botanical wall art prints]]
Pro Tip: Group smaller decor pieces together rather than spreading them thinly across the whole kitchen. A curated cluster of two or three items on one wall feels intentional and styled — scattered items just look random.

Farmhouse Kitchen Furniture and Layout

Getting the furniture and layout right is about balancing practicality with that signature farmhouse warmth. This is not a minimal Scandi kitchen — there should be texture, layers, and a sense of generous living.

The centrepiece for many farmhouse kitchens is a large kitchen table rather than a small breakfast bar. If you've got the space, a scrubbed pine or oak table with mismatched chairs or a mix of chairs and a bench is incredibly characterful and genuinely usable for family life.

[[IMG|farmhouse-kitchen-furniture-layout|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling unless this section is about another interior style. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A spacious farmhouse kitchen with a large scrubbed oak dining table at its centre, surrounded by a wooden bench on one side and mismatched Windsor chairs on the other. A wicker bread basket, ceramic jug with dried flowers, and simple linen napkins are on the table. The floor is wide-plank oak and the walls are painted in a warm off-white. A White British man in his forties sits at the table reading a newspaper with a cafetière beside him, in a relaxed candid pose.]]

Furniture and Layout Tips

  • Kitchen island — if you have the space, a butcher's block or painted island adds both work surface and character
  • Dresser or hutch — a painted Welsh dresser displaying crockery is an instant farmhouse statement
  • Ladder shelving — a leaning ladder shelf in the corner for cookbooks and jars
  • Bench seating — saves space while adding a relaxed, country-kitchen vibe
  • Avoid matching furniture sets — a slightly eclectic mix of pieces always reads as more authentic farmhouse
  • Keep pathways clear — the layout should feel generous and easy to move through
[[PRODUCT|rustic farmhouse kitchen bench with natural wood finish]]
Real Example: A client in rural Shropshire wanted a farmhouse kitchen but had a compact open-plan space. We swapped the glass dining table for a small, solid oak farmhouse table with two spindle chairs and a short bench. It halved the visual fussiness and doubled the warmth of the room instantly.

Farmhouse Kitchen Lighting Ideas

Lighting is what transforms a farmhouse kitchen from a nice room into a genuinely warm one. Get this wrong and even the most carefully styled space will feel flat — especially in the UK where natural light can be in short supply for most of the year.

Pendant lights are the go-to for farmhouse kitchens. Cluster them over your island or table in black metal, aged brass, or wicker shades. The shape matters — look for dome, bell, or lantern-style pendants rather than anything sleek and cylindrical.

[[IMG|farmhouse-kitchen-lighting-ideas|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling unless this section is about another interior style. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A farmhouse kitchen at dusk lit by three aged brass dome pendant lights hanging in a row over a wooden kitchen island, supplemented by a small wall-mounted iron sconce near the cooker. The warm light casts a golden glow on cream cabinets, a marble-effect stone worktop, and a row of terracotta herb pots on the windowsill. A mixed-ethnicity couple — a Middle Eastern woman and a White British man, both in their thirties — are preparing dinner together at the island in a natural, candid moment.]]

Lighting Layers for a Farmhouse Kitchen

  • Pendant lights — cluster two or three over the island or dining table; aged brass or black metal work best
  • Under-cabinet strip lights — practical and they add warmth to the worktop area
  • Wall sconces — an iron or aged brass sconce near the cooker or by a window adds an authentic farmhouse touch
  • Recessed downlights — keep these on a dimmer so you can soften the overall light level in the evening
  • Bulb choice — always warm white (2700K–3000K) rather than cool white; it makes an enormous difference to the feel
  • Candles and lanterns — a cluster of pillar candles or a lantern on the table completes the look for evenings
[[PRODUCT|aged brass dome pendant light for kitchen island]]
Pro Tip: The quickest lighting upgrade in any farmhouse kitchen costs almost nothing — just replace your bulbs with warm white ones. I've seen rooms that felt completely different after this one change. It's the first thing I tell every client.

Farmhouse Kitchen Flooring and Backsplash

Flooring and backsplash are the two surfaces that do the most heavy lifting in terms of setting the farmhouse tone. They're also the ones most people agonise over, so let me make it simpler for you.

For flooring, the classic choices are wide-plank wood (real or engineered), large stone flags, or terracotta tiles. Each of those brings that sense of history and solidity that farmhouse style is built on. Avoid anything that looks too new or too polished — a little texture and variation in the material is a good thing.

[[IMG|farmhouse-kitchen-flooring-backsplash|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top, then a clear VISUAL comparison (two labelled photos side by side, or simple labelled icons/steps), minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks. Show a side-by-side visual comparison of two farmhouse kitchen flooring options: on the left, wide-plank warm oak engineered wood flooring labelled "Warm Wood Planks — classic, easy underfoot, works with underfloor heating"; on the right, large terracotta-toned stone flag tiles labelled "Stone Flags / Terracotta Tiles — authentic country feel, durable, cool underfoot".]]

Flooring and Backsplash Comparison

Option Farmhouse Vibe Practical Notes
Wide-plank wood / engineered wood High — warm and characterful Works with underfloor heating; easy to clean
Terracotta or stone flags Very high — most authentic look Cold underfoot; needs sealing; long-lasting
Encaustic cement tiles High — great for patterned farmhouse feel Can be pricey; stunning as a backsplash too
Subway tile backsplash Medium — classic but can read as modern Choose off-white or cream rather than stark white
Shiplap / tongue-and-groove backsplash Very high — genuinely rustic Not for behind the hob; works well on other walls
Pro Tip: If you're doing a backsplash on a budget, consider peel-and-stick encaustic-style tiles for a rented kitchen or a quick update. They've improved enormously in quality and you can remove them without damage when you move on.

Wall Art and Printable Decor Specifically Styled for Farmhouse Kitchens

This is the area that most kitchen guides barely touch on, and it's the one that makes the biggest difference to how a farmhouse kitchen actually feels. The right wall art in a kitchen isn't just decorative — it's the thing that tells the story of the space.

Farmhouse kitchen wall art tends to work best when it relates to food, nature, or the countryside — botanical illustrations, herb charts, vintage-style market prints, animal illustrations, or simple typographic pieces in earthy tones. Printable art is a brilliant option here because you can download, print, and frame at whatever size suits your wall, often for very little money.

[[IMG|farmhouse-kitchen-wall-art-printable-decor|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling unless this section is about another interior style. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A farmhouse kitchen corner with a natural linen-painted wall featuring a row of three identical narrow oak floating shelves displaying small botanical ceramic plant pots, dried herb bundles tied with twine, and a small wicker basket. A macramé wall hanging is mounted beside the shelves. The worktop below holds a wooden chopping board and a ceramic utensil holder. A Black British man in his late twenties reaches up to adjust one of the herb pots, in a natural relaxed pose.]]

Best Wall Art Styles for Farmhouse Kitchens

  • Herb chart prints — identifying common herbs with their botanical names; incredibly popular and genuinely useful
  • Vintage market prints — illustrative style vegetables, fruits, or jars in earthy tones
  • Animal illustrations — chickens, cows, pigs, or sheep in a loose watercolour or linocut style
  • Typographic kitchen prints — simple phrases or food-related words in block lettering
  • Botanical illustrations — pressed flower or plant illustrations in a classic engraving style
  • Map prints — a vintage-style map of a local area or favourite countryside region
  • Abstract prints in earthy tones — terracotta, ochre, sage, and cream for a modern farmhouse feel
[[PRODUCT|farmhouse kitchen herb chart botanical art prints]] [[PRODUCT|vintage market vegetable illustration wall art for kitchen]]

I had a client in Edinburgh who felt her newly renovated farmhouse kitchen was "missing something" even after the builders had finished. The worktops, tiles, and cabinets were perfect — but the walls were completely bare. We added a set of three herb chart prints in simple pine frames and a woven wall hanging above the dining bench. She texted me a photo the same evening and said it finally felt like her kitchen. That's the power of wall art — it's the last five per cent that does fifty per cent of the emotional work.

Pro Tip: In a kitchen, frame your art properly — a glazed frame protects prints from steam and cooking smells. Go for glass rather than acrylic if you can, and choose simple natural wood or black metal frames rather than ornate gilt ones.

DIY and Budget-Friendly Farmhouse Kitchen Makeover Tips

You genuinely do not need a large budget to get a beautiful farmhouse kitchen. Some of the best-looking spaces I've styled have been done on a shoestring — it's about knowing where to spend and where to save.

The biggest bang for your buck almost always comes from paint, hardware, and styling rather than structural changes. I've seen a kitchen go from builder's basic to genuinely characterful for well under a few hundred pounds.

Budget-Friendly Farmhouse Kitchen Upgrades

  • Paint your cabinets — the single most impactful change; chalk or mineral paints adhere well to existing doors
  • Swap hardware — new handles are cheap and transformative; look for black iron or aged brass styles
  • Add a floating shelf — a reclaimed wood plank on some simple brackets displays ceramics and plants beautifully
  • Use printable wall art — download, print at a local print shop, and frame with charity shop finds
  • Style your worktops — a wooden bread board, a ceramic jug of wooden spoons, and a small herb plant cost very little
  • Reupholster or slipcover chairs — natural linen or hessian fabric completely changes a dining chair
  • Add a natural fibre rug — a jute or coir runner in a farmhouse kitchen ties the whole floor together
  • Change your light switch plates — replace plastic ones with brushed brass or black iron; it costs almost nothing

Total outlay was modest, and the before-and-after was dramatic. Renting is not an excuse to live with a kitchen you don't love.

How to Mix Modern and Rustic Farmhouse Elements

Pure rustic farmhouse can tip into feeling heavy or dated if you're not careful. Mixing in some modern elements is the key to keeping it fresh and liveable — this is what people mean when they say "modern farmhouse."

The trick is to keep the bones modern and layer the character on top. So you might have sleek integrated appliances (modern), but pair them with shaker cabinet doors (farmhouse), a stone worktop (timeless), and open shelving displaying handmade ceramics (warmth).

Modern vs Rustic — How to Balance Them

  • Keep appliances integrated or sleek — a modern oven and fridge behind clean doors grounds the room
  • Use natural materials as the bridge — stone, wood, and linen work in both worlds
  • Choose art that's contemporary in composition but traditional in subject — a modern abstract in earthy tones reads as farmhouse without being kitschy
  • Mix metals thoughtfully — stick to two at most: aged brass and matte black is a classic combination
  • Let the textiles soften — linen curtains or a woven blind adds the rustic warmth without touching the structure
  • Keep clutter intentional — farmhouse isn't messy; it's curated to look effortlessly lived-in
Pro Tip: The number one mistake in modern farmhouse kitchens is going too rustic on too many things at once. Pick three or four strong rustic elements — a Belfast sink, shaker doors, open shelving, a wooden table — and keep everything else clean and simple around them.

Seasonal and Functional Farmhouse Kitchen Styling

One of the things I love most about farmhouse kitchen decor is how naturally it lends itself to seasonal changes. Because the base palette is neutral and the materials are natural, it's easy to shift the feel of the space with just a few swaps.

This is also where function and beauty really overlap — the farmhouse kitchen is not a showroom. It should work hard, store things beautifully, and change with the seasons in a way that feels genuine rather than forced.

Seasonal Styling by Quarter

  • Spring — fresh herbs in terracotta pots on the windowsill, botanical prints, pale green and yellow accents
  • Summer — a jug of wildflowers on the table, linen napkins in soft blue or white, bowls of seasonal fruit
  • Autumn — dried grasses, pumpkins, warm ochre and rust textiles, a cinnamon stick bundle tied with twine
  • Winter — evergreen sprigs in a ceramic vase, candles on the table, thick woven placemats, a stack of warming cookbooks
  • Year-round functional styling — canisters on open shelves, a wooden knife block, a ceramic utensil crock, a linen peg bag by the door
Pro Tip: You don't need to overhaul the whole room seasonally — just change three things: the textile (table runner or cushion), the living element (plant, flowers, or fruit), and one small decor piece on the shelf. That's genuinely enough to shift the feel of the room.

When people ask me where to start with shopping for farmhouse kitchen decor, I always say: start with what goes on the walls and the surfaces, not the structure. These are the things you can change most easily and they have the most immediate visual impact.

Here's how I'd think about building your farmhouse kitchen decor collection in a sensible order — from the investment pieces to the finishing touches.

Shopping Priority List for Farmhouse Kitchen Decor

  • 1. Wall art — your first and most impactful purchase; choose two or three prints in cohesive tones and subject matter
  • 2. Lighting — upgrade your pendant or add a wall sconce; warm bulbs are non-negotiable
  • 3. Textiles — linen tea towels, a natural runner rug, linen or cotton curtains
  • 4. Ceramics — a handmade or handmade-look mixing bowl, a ceramic utensil crock, some simple plates for open shelving
  • 5. Plants and botanicals — potted herbs, trailing plants, dried grasses, a small wicker basket of pinecones
  • 6. Storage as decor — a wooden bread bin, glass canisters with chalkboard labels, a wicker storage basket
  • 7. Finishing touches — a wooden clock, a small oval mirror, a woven wall hanging

Pro Tip: Always buy your wall art before you buy your textiles and accessories — it's much easier to match a tea towel to a print than to find a print that goes with a tea towel you've already committed to.

How to Decorate a Kitchen Wall Farmhouse Style?

Decorating a kitchen wall farmhouse style is really about layering — not just hanging one thing on a blank wall, but building up texture, depth, and a sense of collected-over-time character.

The key principle is to mix types of wall decor rather than relying on one alone. A print on its own can look isolated. But combine it with a shelf, a hanging plant, and a small mirror, and the whole wall starts to feel like it has a story.

Step-by-Step Kitchen Wall Decorating

  • Step 1 — Choose your anchor piece: a print, a shelf, or a large mirror; this sets the scale for everything else
  • Step 2 — Add a living element: a plant, a herb pot, or a bunch of dried flowers brings the wall to life
  • Step 3 — Introduce texture: a woven hanging, a rattan mirror, or a wicker basket on the wall
  • Step 4 — Use functional pieces: wall hooks, a peg rail, or a mounted clock can be decorative and useful
  • Step 5 — Step back and edit: remove anything that feels cluttered; a farmhouse wall should feel collected, not crowded
Real Example: I always recommend the "three things rule" for a first attempt at kitchen wall decorating: pick one practical item (a peg hook or clock), one natural item (a plant or dried herbs), and one decorative item (a print or mirror). Those three together almost always look good immediately, without requiring any real skill in arrangement.

Modern Farmhouse Kitchen Wall Art

Modern farmhouse kitchen wall art sits right at the intersection of clean contemporary design and traditional country warmth. It's a look that works brilliantly in newer builds or open-plan spaces where everything else is fairly minimal.

The key difference between modern and purely rustic farmhouse wall art is in the execution rather than the subject. Modern farmhouse art tends to have cleaner lines, more negative space, and a more restrained palette — think a single botanical illustration on a white background rather than a full decorative border.

Modern Farmhouse Wall Art — Style Characteristics

  • Clean, uncluttered compositions with generous white space in the design
  • Muted earthy palette — sage, warm white, terracotta, oatmeal, ochre
  • Simple black or natural wood frames rather than ornate gilt
  • Subjects: single botanical illustrations, minimalist typography, abstract shapes in earth tones
  • Gallery walls kept to two or three pieces maximum in matching or closely related frames
  • Digital print and giclée art for crisp quality in a small kitchen space
[[PRODUCT|modern farmhouse kitchen wall art prints in earth tones]]
Pro Tip: For a modern farmhouse kitchen, choose ONE dominant art style and stick to it across your two or three prints. Mixing a loose watercolour with a bold typographic piece and a linocut illustration will make the wall feel chaotic rather than curated.

Rustic Farmhouse Kitchen Wall Art

If modern farmhouse leans clean and restrained, rustic farmhouse wall art goes the other way — it's warmer, more layered, and leans into the aged-and-loved aesthetic. Think vintage market posters, hand-lettered signs, old botanical engravings, and animal illustrations.

Rustic farmhouse kitchen wall art pairs best with the more traditional elements: a Belfast sink, shiplap walls, an Aga or range cooker, flagstone floors. If you've got these in your kitchen, go for it — the more decorative and characterful the wall art, the better it will work.

Rustic Farmhouse Wall Art — Ideas and Pairings

  • Vintage botanical engravings — printed on aged-looking paper and framed in distressed wood
  • Hand-lettered farm signs — a slate or wooden plaque with a simple countryside phrase
  • Animal illustrations — chickens or cows in a folk-art or linocut print style
  • Antique-style recipe or market prints — look for sepia tones or aged paper backgrounds
  • Framed hessian or linen embroidery — a simple cross-stitch piece in a plain wooden frame
  • Rustic wall-mounted shelves with decorative pieces — the shelf itself becomes part of the display

Pro Tip: With rustic farmhouse wall art, the frames are as important as the prints. Look for reclaimed, distressed, or unfinished wood frames rather than smooth painted ones — the texture of the frame adds to the overall aged character of the piece.

Farmhouse Kitchen Home Decor Ideas

When people say they want farmhouse kitchen home decor ideas, they usually mean they want the whole picture — not just one element, but how everything works together as a complete look. So let me give you that overview.

Think of your farmhouse kitchen decor in three layers: the structural layer (cabinets, flooring, tiles), the furniture and textile layer (table, chairs, rugs, curtains), and the styling layer (art, plants, ceramics, candles). You can work on any layer independently, but the magic happens when all three are pulling in the same direction.

Farmhouse Kitchen Decor — The Three Layers

  • Layer 1 — Structural: cabinet style and colour, flooring, tiles, backsplash, sink and taps
  • Layer 2 — Furniture and Textiles: table, chairs, bench, rug, curtains or blinds, linen napkins and tea towels
  • Layer 3 — Styling: wall art, plants, ceramics, candles, dried botanicals, baskets, books, clocks
  • Start with Layer 3 if you're on a budget — it has the most visual impact for the least outlay
  • Keep the palette consistent across all three layers: warm neutrals, natural wood, and two or three earthy accent colours
Real Example: I always tell people: if you walked into the room and took away all the styling — the art, the plants, the textiles — would it still feel like a farmhouse kitchen? If not, your structural layer needs attention. If yes, then your styling layer is what takes it from nice to truly special.

Modern Farmhouse Kitchen Home Decor

Modern farmhouse kitchen home decor is essentially the edited, contemporary version of the classic country kitchen. It keeps all the warmth and natural material appeal but strips back the fussiness and the overtly rustic details.

If you live in a newer home or an apartment, this is probably the version that will work best for you. The bones of your kitchen are likely already clean-lined, so you're adding warmth and character to something that starts fairly minimal.

A linen Roman blind hangs at the window and a small oval rattan mirror is on the wall beside it. Modern Farmhouse Decor Hallmarks

  • Clean-lined cabinets (shaker or even flat-panel) in muted tones — sage, warm white, oatmeal
  • Mixed textures rather than mixed patterns — wood, ceramic, linen, rattan, stone
  • Minimal clutter; every item on the worktop or shelf is intentional and beautiful
  • Wall art that's restrained in composition — fewer pieces, more impact
  • Natural plants as a key styling tool — a trailing plant on a shelf does enormous work
  • Warm lighting — always warm white bulbs; never cool white in a modern farmhouse kitchen
Pro Tip: The quickest way to modernise a farmhouse kitchen that's feeling a bit heavy is to remove things rather than add them. Clear two thirds of your open shelves, keep only the most beautiful pieces, and the room will instantly feel lighter and more contemporary.

Rustic Farmhouse Kitchen Home Decor

Rustic farmhouse kitchen home decor is the full, unedited version — and honestly, in the right house, it's absolutely glorious. We're talking flagstone floors, exposed beams, a Belfast sink, a range cooker, and walls full of character and warmth.

The challenge with full rustic farmhouse decor is making it feel curated rather than cluttered. Because there are so many potential elements — ceramics, textiles, art, plants, baskets, pottery — it can easily tip over into chaos if you're not disciplined about the palette and the composition of each display.

Rustic Farmhouse Decor — Key Principles

  • Anchor the room with one large statement piece: a Welsh dresser, a range cooker, or a Belfast sink
  • Stick to a palette of no more than four tones: typically cream, warm wood, one earthy accent, and black iron
  • Group items by material: all your pottery together, all your baskets together, all your botanicals together
  • Use texture as your main decorative tool — rough stone, smooth ceramic, coarse linen, rough-hewn wood
  • Bring in living things: herbs in terracotta pots, a trailing plant on a high shelf, dried flowers in a jug
  • Wall decor: keep it warm and characterful — wicker, iron, wood and botanical prints all work beautifully
Pro Tip: With rustic farmhouse decor, odd numbers almost always look better than even ones. Three ceramic jugs on a shelf is more pleasing than two or four. Five hooks in a row is better than six. It's a small thing, but it makes a real difference to how display arrangements read.

Farmhouse Kitchen and Living Room Decor — Creating Flow Between Spaces

Open-plan living is so common in UK homes now that the question of how to connect the farmhouse kitchen home decor living room space is a really practical one. The challenge is making the two spaces feel unified without making them look identical.

The key is what I call a "shared thread" — a consistent palette, a repeated material, or a matching art style that runs through both rooms. The kitchen and living room don't need to match perfectly, but they should clearly belong to the same house.

[[IMG|farmhouse-kitchen-living-room-decor-flow|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling unless this section is about another interior style. The wall colour — a warm off-white — runs continuously through both spaces, unifying them. Creating Farmhouse Continuity Between Kitchen and Living Room

  • Shared wall colour — the same paint running through both spaces is the simplest way to create unity
  • Repeated material — if you have oak shelving in the kitchen, bring oak into the living room with a coffee table or side table
  • Matching art style — botanical prints in the kitchen, botanical prints in the living room, same frame style throughout
  • Shared textile colour — a colour that appears in a kitchen textile (a sage green linen blind) echoes in a living room cushion
  • Consistent lighting tone — warm white bulbs in both spaces, similar lamp and fitting styles
  • Plants as connectors — trailing plants on kitchen shelves and a large floor plant in the living corner create visual continuity

Pro Tip: If you're unsure whether your kitchen and living room are speaking to each other, take a photo from across the whole open-plan space and look at it on your phone. The photo will show you very quickly whether the two zones feel like one home or two different rooms fighting for attention.

More About Farmhouse Kitchens — What the Experts Say

The farmhouse kitchen trend shows no signs of slowing, and the reason is simple: it's a style that's genuinely warm and genuinely functional, which is a rare combination in interior design.

What I find interesting is that the best examples of farmhouse kitchens all share the same quality — they look like they've been built up slowly over time by someone who actually cooks and lives in the room. That sense of authenticity is something you can absolutely create intentionally, and it's what this whole guide is about. If you want to go deeper on the structural and design side of things, the team at Farmhouse kitchen ideas at Homes & Gardens have put together a thorough overview of the key design decisions involved — it's well worth a read alongside this guide.

The thing that most guides miss, and what I really hope this one makes clear, is that the wall art, the styling accessories, and the small decorative choices are not afterthoughts. They're the difference between a kitchen that looks good in a photo and a kitchen that actually feels incredible to be in every single day. That's the difference I'm always trying to help people achieve.

Let's Keep the Conversation Going

I hope this guide has given you a genuinely useful, practical starting point for building the farmhouse kitchen you've been picturing. Whether you're just adding a few prints and a new pendant light, or you're in the middle of a full kitchen renovation, there's something here for every stage and every budget.

The most important thing I want you to take away is that the warmth of a farmhouse kitchen doesn't come from any one big-ticket decision — it comes from the accumulation of small, thoughtful choices, right down to the art on the walls and the texture of the rug underfoot. Those details are what make a space feel like home.

So I'd love to know — what's the one element of your kitchen you most want to change first? Is it the walls, the lighting, the colours, or something else entirely? Drop a comment and let me know — I genuinely read every one.

- Textiles: jute and seagrass round or layered rugs, diamond-weave cushions in olive gold and tobacco, chunky linen or cotton throws in oatmeal and warm grey, all with visible texture and artisan weave character
- Mood: grounded, handcrafted, unhurried
- White balance: Warm white balance — walls and surfaces read golden-sand rather than cool white, with no blue or grey cast but without tipping into amber
- No: high-gloss or shiny lacquered furniture, cool grey or blue tones, minimalist Scandi white, chrome or polished nickel hardware, mass-produced plastic or resin objects, tropical or lush greenery, neon or saturated accent colours

Quiz notes: none

farmhouse kitchen ideas.finishedBody:
Farmhouse kitchen ideas are having a real moment right now, and honestly, it's easy to see why — that warm, lived-in, slightly rustic look just makes a kitchen feel like the heart of the home. Whether you're starting from scratch or trying to refresh what you've already got, there's so much you can do beyond swapping out cabinet handles. In this guide, I'm going to walk you through every layer of the farmhouse kitchen look, from flooring to wall art to lighting, so you can build a space that actually feels like yours.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever walked into someone's kitchen and just thought, "I want to live here"? That feeling almost always comes down to the details — the textures, the colours, the little touches on the walls. It's exactly why I think wall art and decorative styling are the most underrated tools in any kitchen makeover. Most people focus on the big-ticket items and then wonder why the space still feels a bit flat.

Quick answer: The best farmhouse kitchen ideas combine natural materials, muted earthy tones, and warm lighting with carefully chosen wall art, prints, and styling accessories. You don't need to gut your kitchen — targeted changes to walls, furniture, and decor can completely shift the feel of the space.

Farmhouse style in the kitchen is all about warmth, practicality, and a sense that the room has been lived in and loved over time. It draws on traditional country aesthetics — think shiplap, butler sinks, open shelving, and natural wood — but it doesn't have to feel dated or heavy. If you're looking for unique wall art that fits a farmhouse kitchen or some unique home decor to pull the whole look together, I've got you covered throughout this guide.
