Farmhouse Kitchen Cabinet and Color Ideas

Your cabinets and colour palette are the foundation of the whole farmhouse kitchen look, so it's worth getting these right before anything else. The good news is you have a lot of options, whether you're painting existing units or starting fresh.

Classic farmhouse cabinet colours sit firmly in the muted, earthy camp — think off-white, warm cream, sage green, dusty blue, or soft taupe. These shades work because they don't fight with the natural materials (wood, stone, linen) that the style relies on. I generally steer clients away from stark white because it reads as modern rather than farmhouse.

Cabinet and Colour Quick Guide

  • Shaker-style doors — the most versatile cabinet style for farmhouse; works in both rustic and modern versions
  • Off-white or cream — timeless and pairs beautifully with warm wood accents
  • Sage green — popular right now and reads as both modern and traditionally farmhouse
  • Dusty navy — a bolder option for lower cabinets that adds depth without going dark
  • Open shelving — replace a few upper cabinet doors with open shelves to display ceramics and jars
  • Mixed finishes — two-tone cabinets (different uppers and lowers) add character
  • Hardware — brushed brass, black iron, or aged bronze handles all suit the style

I once helped a client in Surrey who had a kitchen full of glossy white cabinets and couldn't understand why it felt clinical. We simply painted the lower units in a warm linen tone and replaced the chrome handles with black cast-iron bar pulls. The transformation cost very little but completely shifted the feeling of the room.

Pro Tip: If you're renting or on a tight budget, cabinet paint is your best friend. A good chalk-based paint in a heritage shade can completely change the character of your kitchen without a single structural change — and it's reversible.

Farmhouse Kitchen Decor and Wall Art

This is where I get really excited, because farmhouse kitchen decor is so much more than just a few enamel signs and a fruit bowl. The walls, the shelves, the surfaces — every inch is an opportunity to build warmth and personality into the space.

The mistake I always see is people decorating their entire kitchen and then leaving the walls completely bare. It's the equivalent of getting dressed and forgetting your shoes. The walls are what make a kitchen feel complete and cohesive.

Farmhouse Kitchen Decor Must-Haves

  • Botanical or botanical-inspired prints in simple wooden or black frames
  • Typographic prints with kitchen phrases, herb names, or countryside motifs
  • Woven wall hangings or macramé in natural cotton or jute
  • Mounted wooden shelves displaying ceramics and trailing plants
  • Enamel or vintage-look signs used sparingly as a focal accent
  • Clocks with rustic metal or wooden frames
  • Small mirrors with distressed or natural wood frames to bounce light

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: Group smaller decor pieces together rather than spreading them thinly across the whole kitchen. A curated cluster of two or three items on one wall feels intentional and styled — scattered items just look random.

Farmhouse Kitchen Furniture and Layout

Getting the furniture and layout right is about balancing practicality with that signature farmhouse warmth. This is not a minimal Scandi kitchen — there should be texture, layers, and a sense of generous living.

The centrepiece for many farmhouse kitchens is a large kitchen table rather than a small breakfast bar. If you've got the space, a scrubbed pine or oak table with mismatched chairs or a mix of chairs and a bench is incredibly characterful and genuinely usable for family life.

Furniture and Layout Tips

  • Kitchen island — if you have the space, a butcher's block or painted island adds both work surface and character
  • Dresser or hutch — a painted Welsh dresser displaying crockery is an instant farmhouse statement
  • Ladder shelving — a leaning ladder shelf in the corner for cookbooks and jars
  • Bench seating — saves space while adding a relaxed, country-kitchen vibe
  • Avoid matching furniture sets — a slightly eclectic mix of pieces always reads as more authentic farmhouse
  • Keep pathways clear — the layout should feel generous and easy to move through

SHOP HERE
Real Example: A client in rural Shropshire wanted a farmhouse kitchen but had a compact open-plan space. We swapped the glass dining table for a small, solid oak farmhouse table with two spindle chairs and a short bench. It halved the visual fussiness and doubled the warmth of the room instantly.

Farmhouse Kitchen Lighting Ideas

Lighting is what transforms a farmhouse kitchen from a nice room into a genuinely warm one. Get this wrong and even the most carefully styled space will feel flat — especially in the UK where natural light can be in short supply for most of the year.

Pendant lights are the go-to for farmhouse kitchens. Cluster them over your island or table in black metal, aged brass, or wicker shades. The shape matters — look for dome, bell, or lantern-style pendants rather than anything sleek and cylindrical.

Lighting Layers for a Farmhouse Kitchen

  • Pendant lights — cluster two or three over the island or dining table; aged brass or black metal work best
  • Under-cabinet strip lights — practical and they add warmth to the worktop area
  • Wall sconces — an iron or aged brass sconce near the cooker or by a window adds an authentic farmhouse touch
  • Recessed downlights — keep these on a dimmer so you can soften the overall light level in the evening
  • Bulb choice — always warm white (2700K–3000K) rather than cool white; it makes an enormous difference to the feel
  • Candles and lanterns — a cluster of pillar candles or a lantern on the table completes the look for evenings

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: The quickest lighting upgrade in any farmhouse kitchen costs almost nothing — just replace your bulbs with warm white ones. I've seen rooms that felt completely different after this one change. It's the first thing I tell every client.

Farmhouse Kitchen Flooring and Backsplash

Flooring and backsplash are the two surfaces that do the most heavy lifting in terms of setting the farmhouse tone. They're also the ones most people agonise over, so let me make it simpler for you.

For flooring, the classic choices are wide-plank wood (real or engineered), large stone flags, or terracotta tiles. Each of those brings that sense of history and solidity that farmhouse style is built on. Avoid anything that looks too new or too polished — a little texture and variation in the material is a good thing.

Flooring and Backsplash Comparison

Option Farmhouse Vibe Practical Notes
Wide-plank wood / engineered wood High — warm and characterful Works with underfloor heating; easy to clean
Terracotta or stone flags Very high — most authentic look Cold underfoot; needs sealing; long-lasting
Encaustic cement tiles High — great for patterned farmhouse feel Can be pricey; stunning as a backsplash too
Subway tile backsplash Medium — classic but can read as modern Choose off-white or cream rather than stark white
Shiplap / tongue-and-groove backsplash Very high — genuinely rustic Not for behind the hob; works well on other walls
Pro Tip: If you're doing a backsplash on a budget, consider peel-and-stick encaustic-style tiles for a rented kitchen or a quick update. They've improved enormously in quality and you can remove them without damage when you move on.

Wall Art and Printable Decor Specifically Styled for Farmhouse Kitchens

This is the area that most kitchen guides barely touch on, and it's the one that makes the biggest difference to how a farmhouse kitchen actually feels. The right wall art in a kitchen isn't just decorative — it's the thing that tells the story of the space.

Farmhouse kitchen wall art tends to work best when it relates to food, nature, or the countryside — botanical illustrations, herb charts, vintage-style market prints, animal illustrations, or simple typographic pieces in earthy tones. Printable art is a brilliant option here because you can download, print, and frame at whatever size suits your wall, often for very little money.

Best Wall Art Styles for Farmhouse Kitchens

  • Herb chart prints — identifying common herbs with their botanical names; incredibly popular and genuinely useful
  • Vintage market prints — illustrative style vegetables, fruits, or jars in earthy tones
  • Animal illustrations — chickens, cows, pigs, or sheep in a loose watercolour or linocut style
  • Typographic kitchen prints — simple phrases or food-related words in block lettering
  • Botanical illustrations — pressed flower or plant illustrations in a classic engraving style
  • Map prints — a vintage-style map of a local area or favourite countryside region
  • Abstract prints in earthy tones — terracotta, ochre, sage, and cream for a modern farmhouse feel

SHOP HERE

SHOP HERE

I had a client in Edinburgh who felt her newly renovated farmhouse kitchen was "missing something" even after the builders had finished. The worktops, tiles, and cabinets were perfect — but the walls were completely bare. We added a set of three herb chart prints in simple pine frames and a woven wall hanging above the dining bench. She texted me a photo the same evening and said it finally felt like her kitchen. That's the power of wall art — it's the last five per cent that does fifty per cent of the emotional work.

Pro Tip: In a kitchen, frame your art properly — a glazed frame protects prints from steam and cooking smells. Go for glass rather than acrylic if you can, and choose simple natural wood or black metal frames rather than ornate gilt ones.

DIY and Budget-Friendly Farmhouse Kitchen Makeover Tips

You genuinely do not need a large budget to get a beautiful farmhouse kitchen. Some of the best-looking spaces I've styled have been done on a shoestring — it's about knowing where to spend and where to save.

The biggest bang for your buck almost always comes from paint, hardware, and styling rather than structural changes. I've seen a kitchen go from builder's basic to genuinely characterful for well under a few hundred pounds.

Budget-Friendly Farmhouse Kitchen Upgrades

  • Paint your cabinets — the single most impactful change; chalk or mineral paints adhere well to existing doors
  • Swap hardware — new handles are cheap and transformative; look for black iron or aged brass styles
  • Add a floating shelf — a reclaimed wood plank on some simple brackets displays ceramics and plants beautifully
  • Use printable wall art — download, print at a local print shop, and frame with charity shop finds
  • Style your worktops — a wooden bread board, a ceramic jug of wooden spoons, and a small herb plant cost very little
  • Reupholster or slipcover chairs — natural linen or hessian fabric completely changes a dining chair
  • Add a natural fibre rug — a jute or coir runner in a farmhouse kitchen ties the whole floor together
  • Change your light switch plates — replace plastic ones with brushed brass or black iron; it costs almost nothing

SHOP HERE
Real Example: Here's what happened when I tried a full farmhouse styling on a rented kitchen with no structural changes allowed: cabinet paint, new handles, three floating shelves from a reclaimed wood supplier, a jute runner, and a set of botanical prints. Total outlay was modest, and the before-and-after was dramatic. Renting is not an excuse to live with a kitchen you don't love.

How to Mix Modern and Rustic Farmhouse Elements

Pure rustic farmhouse can tip into feeling heavy or dated if you're not careful. Mixing in some modern elements is the key to keeping it fresh and liveable — this is what people mean when they say "modern farmhouse."

The trick is to keep the bones modern and layer the character on top. So you might have sleek integrated appliances (modern), but pair them with shaker cabinet doors (farmhouse), a stone worktop (timeless), and open shelving displaying handmade ceramics (warmth).

Modern vs Rustic — How to Balance Them

  • Keep appliances integrated or sleek — a modern oven and fridge behind clean doors grounds the room
  • Use natural materials as the bridge — stone, wood, and linen work in both worlds
  • Choose art that's contemporary in composition but traditional in subject — a modern abstract in earthy tones reads as farmhouse without being kitschy
  • Mix metals thoughtfully — stick to two at most: aged brass and matte black is a classic combination
  • Let the textiles soften — linen curtains or a woven blind adds the rustic warmth without touching the structure
  • Keep clutter intentional — farmhouse isn't messy; it's curated to look effortlessly lived-in
Pro Tip: The number one mistake in modern farmhouse kitchens is going too rustic on too many things at once. Pick three or four strong rustic elements — a Belfast sink, shaker doors, open shelving, a wooden table — and keep everything else clean and simple around them.

Seasonal and Functional Farmhouse Kitchen Styling

One of the things I love most about farmhouse kitchen decor is how naturally it lends itself to seasonal changes. Because the base palette is neutral and the materials are natural, it's easy to shift the feel of the space with just a few swaps.

This is also where function and beauty really overlap — the farmhouse kitchen is not a showroom. It should work hard, store things beautifully, and change with the seasons in a way that feels genuine rather than forced.

Seasonal Styling by Quarter

  • Spring — fresh herbs in terracotta pots on the windowsill, botanical prints, pale green and yellow accents
  • Summer — a jug of wildflowers on the table, linen napkins in soft blue or white, bowls of seasonal fruit
  • Autumn — dried grasses, pumpkins, warm ochre and rust textiles, a cinnamon stick bundle tied with twine
  • Winter — evergreen sprigs in a ceramic vase, candles on the table, thick woven placemats, a stack of warming cookbooks
  • Year-round functional styling — canisters on open shelves, a wooden knife block, a ceramic utensil crock, a linen peg bag by the door
Pro Tip: You don't need to overhaul the whole room seasonally — just change three things: the textile (table runner or cushion), the living element (plant, flowers, or fruit), and one small decor piece on the shelf. That's genuinely enough to shift the feel of the room.

Farmhouse Kitchen Decor Shopping Guide with Product Recommendations

When people ask me where to start with shopping for farmhouse kitchen decor, I always say: start with what goes on the walls and the surfaces, not the structure. These are the things you can change most easily and they have the most immediate visual impact.

Here's how I'd think about building your farmhouse kitchen decor collection in a sensible order — from the investment pieces to the finishing touches.

Shopping Priority List for Farmhouse Kitchen Decor

  • 1. Wall art — your first and most impactful purchase; choose two or three prints in cohesive tones and subject matter
  • 2. Lighting — upgrade your pendant or add a wall sconce; warm bulbs are non-negotiable
  • 3. Textiles — linen tea towels, a natural runner rug, linen or cotton curtains
  • 4. Ceramics — a handmade or handmade-look mixing bowl, a ceramic utensil crock, some simple plates for open shelving
  • 5. Plants and botanicals — potted herbs, trailing plants, dried grasses, a small wicker basket of pinecones
  • 6. Storage as decor — a wooden bread bin, glass canisters with chalkboard labels, a wicker storage basket
  • 7. Finishing touches — a wooden clock, a small oval mirror, a woven wall hanging

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: Always buy your wall art before you buy your textiles and accessories — it's much easier to match a tea towel to a print than to find a print that goes with a tea towel you've already committed to.

How to Decorate a Kitchen Wall Farmhouse Style?

Decorating a kitchen wall farmhouse style is really about layering — not just hanging one thing on a blank wall, but building up texture, depth, and a sense of collected-over-time character.

The key principle is to mix types of wall decor rather than relying on one alone. A print on its own can look isolated. But combine it with a shelf, a hanging plant, and a small mirror, and the whole wall starts to feel like it has a story.

Step-by-Step Kitchen Wall Decorating

  • Step 1 — Choose your anchor piece: a print, a shelf, or a large mirror; this sets the scale for everything else
  • Step 2 — Add a living element: a plant, a herb pot, or a bunch of dried flowers brings the wall to life
  • Step 3 — Introduce texture: a woven hanging, a rattan mirror, or a wicker basket on the wall
  • Step 4 — Use functional pieces: wall hooks, a peg rail, or a mounted clock can be decorative and useful
  • Step 5 — Step back and edit: remove anything that feels cluttered; a farmhouse wall should feel collected, not crowded
Real Example: I always recommend the "three things rule" for a first attempt at kitchen wall decorating: pick one practical item (a peg hook or clock), one natural item (a plant or dried herbs), and one decorative item (a print or mirror). Those three together almost always look good immediately, without requiring any real skill in arrangement.

Modern Farmhouse Kitchen Wall Art

Modern farmhouse kitchen wall art sits right at the intersection of clean contemporary design and traditional country warmth. It's a look that works brilliantly in newer builds or open-plan spaces where everything else is fairly minimal.

The key difference between modern and purely rustic farmhouse wall art is in the execution rather than the subject. Modern farmhouse art tends to have cleaner lines, more negative space, and a more restrained palette — think a single botanical illustration on a white background rather than a full decorative border.

Modern Farmhouse Wall Art — Style Characteristics

  • Clean, uncluttered compositions with generous white space in the design
  • Muted earthy palette — sage, warm white, terracotta, oatmeal, ochre
  • Simple black or natural wood frames rather than ornate gilt
  • Subjects: single botanical illustrations, minimalist typography, abstract shapes in earth tones
  • Gallery walls kept to two or three pieces maximum in matching or closely related frames
  • Digital print and giclée art for crisp quality in a small kitchen space

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: For a modern farmhouse kitchen, choose ONE dominant art style and stick to it across your two or three prints. Mixing a loose watercolour with a bold typographic piece and a linocut illustration will make the wall feel chaotic rather than curated.

Rustic Farmhouse Kitchen Wall Art

If modern farmhouse leans clean and restrained, rustic farmhouse wall art goes the other way — it's warmer, more layered, and leans into the aged-and-loved aesthetic. Think vintage market posters, hand-lettered signs, old botanical engravings, and animal illustrations.

Rustic farmhouse kitchen wall art pairs best with the more traditional elements: a Belfast sink, shiplap walls, an Aga or range cooker, flagstone floors. If you've got these in your kitchen, go for it — the more decorative and characterful the wall art, the better it will work.

Rustic Farmhouse Wall Art — Ideas and Pairings

  • Vintage botanical engravings — printed on aged-looking paper and framed in distressed wood
  • Hand-lettered farm signs — a slate or wooden plaque with a simple countryside phrase
  • Animal illustrations — chickens or cows in a folk-art or linocut print style
  • Antique-style recipe or market prints — look for sepia tones or aged paper backgrounds
  • Framed hessian or linen embroidery — a simple cross-stitch piece in a plain wooden frame
  • Rustic wall-mounted shelves with decorative pieces — the shelf itself becomes part of the display

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: With rustic farmhouse wall art, the frames are as important as the prints. Look for reclaimed, distressed, or unfinished wood frames rather than smooth painted ones — the texture of the frame adds to the overall aged character of the piece.

Farmhouse Kitchen Home Decor Ideas

When people say they want farmhouse kitchen home decor ideas, they usually mean they want the whole picture — not just one element, but how everything works together as a complete look. So let me give you that overview.

Think of your farmhouse kitchen decor in three layers: the structural layer (cabinets, flooring, tiles), the furniture and textile layer (table, chairs, rugs, curtains), and the styling layer (art, plants, ceramics, candles). You can work on any layer independently, but the magic happens when all three are pulling in the same direction.

Farmhouse Kitchen Decor — The Three Layers

  • Layer 1 — Structural: cabinet style and colour, flooring, tiles, backsplash, sink and taps
  • Layer 2 — Furniture and Textiles: table, chairs, bench, rug, curtains or blinds, linen napkins and tea towels
  • Layer 3 — Styling: wall art, plants, ceramics, candles, dried botanicals, baskets, books, clocks
  • Start with Layer 3 if you're on a budget — it has the most visual impact for the least outlay
  • Keep the palette consistent across all three layers: warm neutrals, natural wood, and two or three earthy accent colours
Real Example: I always tell people: if you walked into the room and took away all the styling — the art, the plants, the textiles — would it still feel like a farmhouse kitchen? If not, your structural layer needs attention. If yes, then your styling layer is what takes it from nice to truly special.

Modern Farmhouse Kitchen Home Decor

Modern farmhouse kitchen home decor is essentially the edited, contemporary version of the classic country kitchen. It keeps all the warmth and natural material appeal but strips back the fussiness and the overtly rustic details.

If you live in a newer home or an apartment, this is probably the version that will work best for you. The bones of your kitchen are likely already clean-lined, so you're adding warmth and character to something that starts fairly minimal.

Modern Farmhouse Decor Hallmarks

  • Clean-lined cabinets (shaker or even flat-panel) in muted tones — sage, warm white, oatmeal
  • Mixed textures rather than mixed patterns — wood, ceramic, linen, rattan, stone
  • Minimal clutter; every item on the worktop or shelf is intentional and beautiful
  • Wall art that's restrained in composition — fewer pieces, more impact
  • Natural plants as a key styling tool — a trailing plant on a shelf does enormous work
  • Warm lighting — always warm white bulbs; never cool white in a modern farmhouse kitchen
Pro Tip: The quickest way to modernise a farmhouse kitchen that's feeling a bit heavy is to remove things rather than add them. Clear two thirds of your open shelves, keep only the most beautiful pieces, and the room will instantly feel lighter and more contemporary.

Rustic Farmhouse Kitchen Home Decor

Rustic farmhouse kitchen home decor is the full, unedited version — and honestly, in the right house, it's absolutely glorious. We're talking flagstone floors, exposed beams, a Belfast sink, a range cooker, and walls full of character and warmth.

The challenge with full rustic farmhouse decor is making it feel curated rather than cluttered. Because there are so many potential elements — ceramics, textiles, art, plants, baskets, pottery — it can easily tip over into chaos if you're not disciplined about the palette and the composition of each display.

Rustic Farmhouse Decor — Key Principles

  • Anchor the room with one large statement piece: a Welsh dresser, a range cooker, or a Belfast sink
  • Stick to a palette of no more than four tones: typically cream, warm wood, one earthy accent, and black iron
  • Group items by material: all your pottery together, all your baskets together, all your botanicals together
  • Use texture as your main decorative tool — rough stone, smooth ceramic, coarse linen, rough-hewn wood
  • Bring in living things: herbs in terracotta pots, a trailing plant on a high shelf, dried flowers in a jug
  • Wall decor: keep it warm and characterful — wicker, iron, wood and botanical prints all work beautifully
Pro Tip: With rustic farmhouse decor, odd numbers almost always look better than even ones. Three ceramic jugs on a shelf is more pleasing than two or four. Five hooks in a row is better than six. It's a small thing, but it makes a real difference to how display arrangements read.

Farmhouse Kitchen and Living Room Decor — Creating Flow Between Spaces

Open-plan living is so common in UK homes now that the question of how to connect the farmhouse kitchen home decor living room space is a really practical one. The challenge is making the two spaces feel unified without making them look identical.

The key is what I call a "shared thread" — a consistent palette, a repeated material, or a matching art style that runs through both rooms. The kitchen and living room don't need to match perfectly, but they should clearly belong to the same house.

Creating Farmhouse Continuity Between Kitchen and Living Room

  • Shared wall colour — the same paint running through both spaces is the simplest way to create unity
  • Repeated material — if you have oak shelving in the kitchen, bring oak into the living room with a coffee table or side table
  • Matching art style — botanical prints in the kitchen, botanical prints in the living room, same frame style throughout
  • Shared textile colour — a colour that appears in a kitchen textile (a sage green linen blind) echoes in a living room cushion
  • Consistent lighting tone — warm white bulbs in both spaces, similar lamp and fitting styles
  • Plants as connectors — trailing plants on kitchen shelves and a large floor plant in the living corner create visual continuity

Pro Tip: If you're unsure whether your kitchen and living room are speaking to each other, take a photo from across the whole open-plan space and look at it on your phone. The photo will show you very quickly whether the two zones feel like one home or two different rooms fighting for attention.

Farmhouse Kitchen Styles and Looks to Inspire You

Whether you're drawn to the clean lines of modern farmhouse or the full texture of a rustic country kitchen, there are so many directions to take this style. Here are some of the looks I find most exciting and liveable right now.

Visual Inspiration

Explore complementary design ideas on our Home Decor by Trend page:

  • Modern Farmhouse Home Decor Trend - rustic charm meets modern simplicity
  • Country Cottage Home Decor Trend - warm cozy countryside kitchen vibes
  • French Country Home Decor Trend - elegant rustic European kitchen style

More About Farmhouse Kitchens — What the Experts Say

The farmhouse kitchen trend shows no signs of slowing, and the reason is simple: it's a style that's genuinely warm and genuinely functional, which is a rare combination in interior design.

What I find interesting is that the best examples of farmhouse kitchens all share the same quality — they look like they've been built up slowly over time by someone who actually cooks and lives in the room. That sense of authenticity is something you can absolutely create intentionally, and it's what this whole guide is about. If you want to go deeper on the structural and design side of things, the team at Farmhouse kitchen ideas at Homes & Gardens have put together a thorough overview of the key design decisions involved — it's well worth a read alongside this guide.

The thing that most guides miss, and what I really hope this one makes clear, is that the wall art, the styling accessories, and the small decorative choices are not afterthoughts. They're the difference between a kitchen that looks good in a photo and a kitchen that actually feels incredible to be in every single day. That's the difference I'm always trying to help people achieve.

WATCH: Farmhouse Kitchen Ideas for Small Spaces

Let's Keep the Conversation Going

I hope this guide has given you a genuinely useful, practical starting point for building the farmhouse kitchen you've been picturing. Whether you're just adding a few prints and a new pendant light, or you're in the middle of a full kitchen renovation, there's something here for every stage and every budget.

The most important thing I want you to take away is that the warmth of a farmhouse kitchen doesn't come from any one big-ticket decision — it comes from the accumulation of small, thoughtful choices, right down to the art on the walls and the texture of the rug underfoot. Those details are what make a space feel like home.

So I'd love to know — what's the one element of your kitchen you most want to change first? Is it the walls, the lighting, the colours, or something else entirely? Drop a comment and let me know — I genuinely read every one.

japandi bedroom.bodyHtml:
A japandi bedroom is one of the most achievable, genuinely calming spaces you can create at home — and you don't need to knock down walls or spend a fortune to get there. It's a blend of Japanese minimalism and Scandinavian cosiness that results in a bedroom that feels both intentional and deeply restful. In this guide I'm going to walk you through every element, from furniture and colour to wall art and plants, so you can build your own version of this look.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever walked into a bedroom and immediately felt your shoulders drop? That instant calm — where everything just feels right — is exactly what good wall art and considered decor can do, and it's precisely the feeling a Japandi bedroom is designed to give you every single day.

Quick answer: A Japandi bedroom combines Japanese wabi-sabi philosophy with Scandinavian hygge warmth to create a serene, clutter-free sleeping space. It uses a neutral palette, natural materials, low-profile furniture, and carefully chosen decor — including wall art — to feel both minimal and liveable. You can achieve the look without a full renovation by updating textiles, art, lighting and accessories.

Japandi as a design style has been gaining real traction in the UK interiors world, and honestly, I think it's because it solves a very real problem: how do you make a room feel genuinely calm without it feeling cold or empty? The answer lies in thoughtful layering of natural textures, warm neutrals, and pieces that have a clear purpose. If you're looking for unique wall art that fits this aesthetic, or unique home decor that brings the whole look together, you're in exactly the right place.

List of Contents

  • Japandi Bedroom Colour Palette and Materials
  • Japandi Bedroom Textiles and Soft Furnishings
  • Japandi Bedroom Storage and Decluttering Principles

  • Best Plants for a Japandi Bedroom

  • More About Japandi Bedroom Design

What is Japandi Style and How Does It Apply to the Bedroom?

Japandi is a design philosophy that merges the best of two distinct cultural aesthetics: Japanese minimalism — rooted in wabi-sabi, the beauty of imperfection — and Scandinavian hygge, which values warmth, simplicity, and functional cosiness. Applied to the bedroom, it means creating a space that is stripped of anything unnecessary, yet never feels stark or unwelcoming.

The bedroom is actually the ideal room to try this style because its whole purpose is rest. Every decision — furniture, colour, light, art — should serve that goal. That's exactly what Japandi thinking demands.

[[IMG|japandi-bedroom-style-overview|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A serene, beautifully styled Japandi bedroom with a low-profile wooden bed frame in pale ash, linen bedding in warm oatmeal tones, a small tatami-style bedside table with a ceramic mug, and a wall-mounted wooden shelf with a small vase and dried grasses. The room has warm, raking morning light from a linen-curtained window. A South Asian woman in her thirties sits cross-legged on the bed, eyes closed, hands resting gently on her knees, in a natural meditative rest pose.]]

Core principles at a glance

  • Less is more — every item earns its place
  • Natural materials only: wood, linen, cotton, ceramic, stone
  • Neutral, earthy tones with no bright accent colours
  • Functionality is never sacrificed for style
  • Imperfections (a knot in wood, a slight texture variation) are celebrated
  • Calm and intention over trend-chasing
Pro Tip: Before you buy a single thing for a Japandi bedroom, take everything out of the room mentally and ask: "Would I miss this if it wasn't here?" If the answer is no, it probably shouldn't be in the room at all.

What Does a Japandi Bedroom Look Like?

A Japandi bedroom looks calm, grounded, and quietly beautiful. The first thing you notice is the absence of clutter — surfaces are clear, there are no decorative objects fighting for attention, and the room has a sense of intentional space. The second thing you notice is the warmth: despite being minimal, it never feels cold.

Visually, expect to see a low wooden bed frame, layered linen bedding in warm neutrals, a few carefully chosen ceramics, natural fibre rugs, and wall art that is understated rather than bold. It's the kind of room that makes you breathe out slowly the moment you walk in.

[[IMG|japandi-bedroom-visual-look|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. Wide-angle view of a complete Japandi bedroom: a low-profile platform bed in natural oak with crumpled warm-white linen, a jute rug on pale timber floorboards, two small ceramic bedside vessels, dried botanicals in a slender vase, and a wooden wall shelf holding a trailing plant. Soft morning light. A Black British man in his early forties and a white British woman in her early forties are standing together near the window in casual home clothes, quietly looking out — relaxed, natural, domestic.]]

Key visual characteristics

  • Low-to-the-ground furniture, especially the bed
  • Warm neutral walls — stone, warm white, greige, soft sage
  • Visible natural grain in wood furniture
  • Textural contrast: smooth ceramics against rough linen, for example
  • A handful of plants, never an overwhelming collection
  • Minimal wall art — usually one or two pieces, well positioned
  • No overhead fluorescent lighting; warm, low, layered light only
Real Example: I had a client in Leeds who kept describing her bedroom as "blah" — she couldn't put her finger on why. It turned out she had three different wood tones, four different shades of beige with no clear logic, and six small decorative items on her dresser that had nothing to do with each other. We removed everything, chose one warm wood tone, and kept just two objects on the dresser. The room felt completely transformed without buying a single new piece of furniture.

Japandi Bedroom Furniture and Layout Essentials

Japandi bedroom furniture is characterised by clean lines, natural materials, and a deliberately low profile. The bed is usually the centrepiece — a simple platform or slat frame in pale ash, oak, or walnut, sitting close to the floor. Bedside tables, if present at all, are small and simple: a solid wood block, a ceramic stool, or a wall-mounted shelf.

Layout matters just as much as the individual pieces. Leave generous space around the bed, avoid pushing every piece of furniture against a wall, and resist the temptation to fill every corner. The empty space is part of the design.

[[IMG|japandi-bedroom-furniture-layout|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A Japandi bedroom showing a low solid-oak platform bed with clean slatted headboard, a small square wooden bedside table, a wooden low-profile dresser with ceramic handles, and clear floorspace around each piece. Light oak flooring, warm white walls, a single trailing plant on a wooden shelf. A mixed-heritage woman in her late thirties is making the bed, smoothing down linen sheets in a natural domestic gesture.]]

Essential Japandi bedroom furniture pieces

  • Bed frame: Low platform, solid or slatted, in pale oak, ash or walnut — no upholstered headboards with heavy nailhead trim
  • Bedside storage: One small side table or wall-mounted shelf per side — keep surfaces minimal
  • Dresser/chest of drawers: Simple, handleless or with ceramic pulls, in a natural wood finish
  • Wardrobe: Flush-door, floor-to-ceiling if possible — avoids visual clutter at the top
  • Seating: Optional — a single low stool or cushioned bench at the foot of the bed if the room allows
[[PRODUCT|japandi low-profile oak platform bed frame]]
Pro Tip: If your existing bed frame is too bulky, try removing the legs if they unscrew, or swap the headboard for a simple padded panel in a neutral linen fabric. Sometimes a small change to the dominant piece shifts the whole room's feel.

Japandi Bedroom Colour Palette and Materials

The Japandi colour palette is intentionally narrow and grounded in nature. Think warm white, soft stone, greige, warm sand, and muted sage — occasionally punctuated by a deeper charcoal or dark espresso in a furniture piece or textural accent. There are no bright, saturated colours anywhere in a true Japandi bedroom.

Materials are equally important. The textures you use carry as much visual weight as the colours. Raw linen, unpolished stone, undyed cotton, pale natural wood with visible grain, and hand-thrown ceramic all belong here. Avoid shiny surfaces, metallic finishes, and synthetic materials wherever possible.

[[IMG|japandi-colour-palette-materials|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top, then a clear VISUAL comparison (two labelled photos side by side, or simple labelled icons/steps), minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks. Show a Japandi colour palette and materials comparison: on the left, a column of colour swatches labelled Warm White, Greige, Warm Sand, Muted Sage, Charcoal — each swatch as a painted brushstroke. On the right, a column of texture swatches labelled Raw Linen, Unpolished Stone, Natural Oak, Hand-thrown Ceramic, Undyed Cotton — each shown as a small square texture tile. Title: "Japandi Bedroom: Colour & Materials".]]

Colour and material dos and don'ts

  • ✓ Warm whites and off-whites (never brilliant white)
  • ✓ Stone, sand, greige, warm taupe
  • ✓ Muted sage, dusty moss, soft olive
  • ✓ One darker anchor tone — charcoal or dark espresso
  • ✗ Bright whites, cool greys, or icy blues
  • ✗ Saturated accent colours — no mustard, terracotta, or teal
  • ✗ High-gloss lacquer, chrome, polished silver finishes
  • ✗ Synthetic textiles — polyester velvet, faux fur, plastic blinds
Pro Tip: Paint the ceiling in the same colour as the walls, or just one shade lighter. It makes the room feel more cocoon-like and cohesive — a trick I've used in every Japandi bedroom I've styled.

Japandi Bedroom Textiles and Soft Furnishings

Textiles are where the Japandi bedroom gets its warmth. The look might be minimal, but it should never feel hard or clinical — and the right soft furnishings are what make the difference. Linen is the star material here: used for bedding, curtains, and even cushion covers, it has that naturally wrinkled, lived-in quality that fits perfectly.

Layer your bedding in similar tones rather than contrasting patterns. A linen duvet cover in warm oatmeal, a cotton waffle throw, and two or three pillows in complementary neutrals is all you need. Resist the urge to pile on cushions — two or three is the absolute maximum.

[[IMG|japandi-bedroom-textiles|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. Close-medium shot of a beautifully made Japandi bed: rumpled linen duvet in warm oatmeal, a folded waffle cotton throw at the foot of the bed in warm greige, two plain linen pillowcases, and a single small ceramic bowl on the bedside surface. Soft raking daylight from the left. A South-East Asian woman in her early thirties is sitting on the edge of the bed, pulling on a sock, completely natural and unposed.]]

Textile checklist for a Japandi bedroom

  • Linen or stonewashed cotton duvet cover — warm neutral tones only
  • A single textural throw — waffle cotton, chunky knit, or bouclé in a tonal colour
  • Two to three linen or cotton pillowcases — no printed patterns
  • A natural fibre rug: jute, seagrass, or a low-pile wool rug in stone or sand
  • Linen or cotton curtains — floor length, unlined or lightly lined, in warm white or greige
  • A small floor cushion or zabuton if you have floor space — nods to the Japanese influence
[[PRODUCT|linen bedding set in warm oatmeal for japandi bedroom]]
Pro Tip: Buy your bedding and curtains from the same colour family, not necessarily the same brand. Holding swatches together in natural light before you buy is the single best thing you can do to avoid a mismatch.

Japandi Bedroom Storage and Decluttering Principles

Hidden storage is fundamental to Japandi. Every object left on display is a deliberate choice — if it's not beautiful or useful, it goes behind a door. This isn't about being cold or sterile; it's about giving the things you do keep room to breathe and be appreciated.

The decluttering approach here borrows from both Japanese concepts — the idea that objects should bring joy and have a clear purpose — and Scandinavian practicality. If a thing doesn't serve the bedroom's purpose (rest and calm), it shouldn't be in the bedroom.

[[IMG|japandi-bedroom-storage|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A neatly styled Japandi bedroom with a floor-to-ceiling flush wardrobe in pale oak veneer, a low wooden chest with minimal ceramic handles, and a single open wooden shelf holding one ceramic vase and one small plant. The floor is completely clear. A tall Black African man in his late thirties is sliding open a wardrobe door, holding a folded linen shirt, in a completely natural everyday gesture.]]

Practical Japandi storage rules

  • Conceal everything you use but don't want to look at: cables, chargers, medication, books
  • Use baskets in natural materials (wicker, seagrass) for things that need to be accessible
  • Limit open shelving — if you have a shelf, it should hold three items maximum
  • Under-bed storage is fine as long as it's in proper boxes or drawers — not random bags
  • If your wardrobe doors are messy or mismatched, consider simple replacement panels in a neutral tone
  • Remove anything from bedside surfaces that isn't essential — one or two items only
Real Example: I once helped a client clear a bedroom in Manchester that had seventeen items on her bedside table. Seventeen. We kept three: a small lamp, a ceramic cup for water, and a single book. She messaged me a week later to say she was sleeping better. I genuinely believe the visual calm of a tidy surface affects how well your brain switches off at night.

Japandi Bedroom Lighting and Accents

Lighting in a Japandi bedroom should always feel warm, low, and layered. Harsh overhead lighting is the enemy of this style — if you have a central ceiling light, put it on a dimmer immediately and use it only when you need to find something. The real atmosphere comes from table lamps, floor lamps, and wall-mounted sconces, all using warm-toned bulbs.

Paper or washi pendant lights, wooden lamp bases, and rattan shades all sit beautifully within the Japandi aesthetic. Accent lighting — a small candle, a low plug-in lamp — adds warmth in the evenings without overwhelming the space.

[[IMG|japandi-bedroom-lighting|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. An intimate evening scene in a Japandi bedroom: a wooden bedside table lamp with a warm amber glow, a Japanese paper pendant light hanging from the ceiling casting a soft diffused halo, a small lit candle on a ceramic plate on the floor, and a wall-mounted wooden sconce. The room has warm stone walls and dark timber floorboards. A South Asian man in his mid-thirties is reading in bed, book held naturally, face lit warmly from the lamp.]]

Japandi lighting guide

  • Ceiling: A single paper or washi pendant on a dimmer — no spotlights, no downlighters if avoidable
  • Bedside: A simple wooden or ceramic-base table lamp with a linen shade
  • Wall: A wooden or rattan wall sconce for ambient accent light
  • Floor: An arching floor lamp in solid wood or matte black for a reading corner
  • Bulbs: Warm white always — 2700K to 3000K, never cool daylight
  • Candles: Unscented or very lightly scented, in ceramic or simple glass vessels
[[PRODUCT|japandi paper pendant ceiling light warm white]]
Pro Tip: Replace a single harsh ceiling bulb with a Japanese paper pendant shade today — it's one of the fastest and cheapest single changes you can make, and it immediately transforms the mood of the entire room.

Japandi Bedroom Wall Art and How to Choose It

Wall art in a Japandi bedroom is about restraint and intention. You're not filling walls — you're making a considered placement of one or two pieces that feel like they belong there. The art itself should feel quiet: nature-inspired, abstract, or graphic in a simple line-work style, in a palette that echoes the room's neutrals.

Avoid anything too busy, overly colourful, or sentimental in the decorative sense. Japandi wall art earns its place by contributing to the calm of the room, not competing with it.

[[IMG|japandi-bedroom-wall-art-selection|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A Japandi bedroom wall styled with a simple wooden floating shelf holding a small ceramic vase with dried grasses, a macramé hanging textile on the wall, and a wall-mounted wooden sconce. Warm stone wall colour, pale timber floor. A mixed-heritage woman in her mid-thirties is considering two items on the shelf, holding one gently, thoughtful expression — a natural styling moment.]]

How to choose Japandi bedroom wall art

  • Choose one to two pieces maximum — single large-format art is often better than a gallery wall
  • Nature subjects work beautifully: botanicals, abstract landscape, water, stone
  • Fine line drawing prints in black ink on warm white paper are quintessentially Japandi
  • Abstract work in earthy neutrals — sand, warm grey, charcoal — fits perfectly
  • Frame in natural materials: pale oak, walnut, or unfinished wood
  • Avoid ornate gold or silver frames, or heavy black plastic
  • Position art at eye level when standing — not too high, not too low
[[PRODUCT|japandi botanical fine line prints for bedroom wall art]]
Pro Tip: If you're unsure about size, cut a piece of brown paper or newspaper to the exact dimensions of the art you're considering and tape it to the wall first. Live with it for a day or two. This five-minute trick has saved many of my clients from expensive mistakes.

What Kind of Wall Art Is Best for a Bedroom?

The best wall art for a bedroom — Japandi or otherwise — is art that helps you switch off. The bedroom is for rest, so the art you choose here should feel different to anything you'd put in a living room or kitchen. Calm, grounding, and personally meaningful without being emotionally intense.

For a Japandi bedroom specifically, the best wall art tends to be understated rather than statement-making. Think subtle over striking.

[[IMG|bedroom-wall-art-types-comparison|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top, then a clear VISUAL comparison (two labelled photos side by side, or simple labelled icons/steps), minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks. Show a comparison of wall art types for a Japandi bedroom: Left column labelled "Best for Japandi Bedroom" showing icons or small vignettes of botanical line art, abstract earth-tone print, simple ink wash landscape. Right column labelled "Avoid in Japandi Bedroom" showing icons or vignettes of brightly coloured pop art, ornate portrait, busy gallery wall. Title: "Choosing Bedroom Wall Art: Japandi vs Not Japandi".]]

Best bedroom wall art types for Japandi

  • Botanical line drawings — single stem, leaf, or branch studies
  • Abstract ink wash prints in black, grey, or warm earth tones
  • Minimal landscape art — a horizon line, distant hills, still water
  • Japanese calligraphy or single kanji characters in a neutral palette
  • Nature photography in muted tones — misty forests, still ponds, stone textures
  • Geometric prints in a very limited palette of two or three neutrals
[[PRODUCT|abstract earth tone bedroom wall art prints japandi]]

What Is Japandi Wall Art?

Japandi wall art is any art that reflects the values of the Japandi aesthetic: simplicity, nature, imperfection, and calm. It tends to draw from Japanese artistic traditions — think sumi-e ink painting, woodblock print influences, negative space, and an appreciation for organic forms — combined with Scandinavian graphic minimalism.

What makes it distinctly Japandi rather than just "minimal" is the warmth. Pure Scandinavian design can trend cold. Japandi wall art always has a human, natural, slightly imperfect quality to it. A brushstroke that isn't perfectly straight. A line drawing with slightly variable weight. That's the wabi-sabi coming through.

[[IMG|japandi-wall-art-definition|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A warm Japandi bedroom corner showing a wooden floating shelf with a single handmade ceramic pot, a dried grass arrangement, and a washi paper wall hanging with a simple ink brushstroke motif. The wall is warm stone, floor is light timber. A Japanese-heritage woman in her late twenties sits at a low wooden desk below the shelf, writing in a notebook with a focused, peaceful expression.]]

Defining features of Japandi wall art

  • Subject matter rooted in nature — plants, water, stone, sky
  • Generous use of negative space — the art doesn't fill every inch of the frame
  • Muted, earthy palette with no bright or saturated colours
  • A handmade quality — slight irregularity is a feature, not a flaw
  • Minimal framing that doesn't compete with the art itself
  • Influence from both Japanese sumi-e tradition and Nordic graphic design
Pro Tip: If you find a print you love but you're not sure if it's "Japandi enough", hold it next to a plain warm white piece of card. If it still feels calm and unhurried in that context, it'll work in a Japandi bedroom.

Modern Japandi Bedroom Wall Art: Styles and Ideas

Modern Japandi bedroom wall art takes the classic Japandi aesthetic and applies a slightly more contemporary lens — think cleaner lines, bolder use of negative space, and occasionally a more graphic quality to the composition. It sits comfortably in a newer-build home or a bedroom that's been styled with a slightly more modern edge.

The key difference from the broader Japandi category is that modern Japandi wall art might lean slightly more towards graphic minimalism — a single bold botanical silhouette in charcoal on warm white, or a precisely composed abstract print — while still retaining that natural warmth and restraint.

[[IMG|modern-japandi-bedroom-wall-art|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A contemporary Japandi bedroom with a low platform bed in pale ash, warm white walls, a wooden floating wall shelf above the headboard holding two ceramic pieces and a small trailing plant, and a wall-mounted wooden sconce. The room has clean, modern lines but natural warm materials. A young Black British woman in her late twenties is arranging a small ceramic on the shelf, standing beside the bed in relaxed home clothes.]]

Modern Japandi wall art ideas to try

  • A single oversized botanical silhouette print above the bed — simple, graphic, serene
  • A diptych (two matching prints side by side) in a tonal palette — stone and charcoal
  • A contemporary ink wash abstract in warm sand and black tones
  • A minimal mountain or horizon line print — graphic but nature-rooted
  • A large-format single-colour abstract in warm white with a slightly textured appearance
  • Fine line botanical studies in a modern narrow wood frame
[[PRODUCT|modern japandi botanical silhouette oversized wall art print]]

Japandi Bedroom Wall Art Ideas for Every Budget

One of the things I genuinely love about Japandi wall art ideas is that they scale beautifully across budgets. Because the aesthetic values simplicity and restraint, you don't need to spend a lot — you need to choose carefully. A single well-chosen, well-framed print does more for a Japandi bedroom than six mediocre pieces ever could.

The mistake I always see is people buying lots of small, cheap prints and hanging them in a gallery wall format. That's not Japandi — that's maximalism in disguise. One strong piece, properly framed and thoughtfully placed, is always the right call.

[[IMG|japandi-wall-art-ideas|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A simple Japandi bedroom showing a wooden wall-mounted shelf above a low platform bed with one ceramic vessel, one dried stem arrangement, and a small hanging textile piece. Warm white walls, pale timber floor, linen bedding. A mixed-race couple — a Chinese-heritage man and a white woman, both in their early thirties — are looking at the shelf together, the woman pointing at one of the objects, both smiling naturally.]]

Japandi bedroom wall art ideas by approach

  • Investment piece: One large original print or limited edition — goes above the bed, becomes the room's focal point
  • Mid-range: A quality fine art print in a natural wood frame — botanical, abstract, or ink wash
  • Budget-friendly: A single high-quality digital print in a simple frame from a local framer
  • DIY: Mount a piece of natural washi paper with a simple ink brushstroke — genuinely beautiful and costs very little
  • Alternative to framed art: A macramé or woven textile hanging — adds texture and is very Japandi
  • Photography: Your own nature photography printed large and simply framed can be stunning
Pro Tip: Spend the same amount on the frame as on the print. A cheap print in a great natural wood frame looks ten times better than a beautiful print in a cheap plastic frame. Framing is never the place to cut corners.

Japandi Bedroom Home Decor Ideas That Actually Work

Japandi bedroom home decor ideas are most effective when they work as a system rather than individual purchases. The question isn't just "is this nice?" — it's "does this belong in this room alongside everything else?" Every single decor item should earn its place.

Some of the most impactful Japandi bedroom home decor ideas are incredibly simple: a single ceramic vase with dried grasses on a shelf, a folded linen throw at the foot of the bed, a small wooden tray to corral the two items allowed on a bedside surface. These are small decisions with a big cumulative effect.

Japandi bedroom home decor ideas that really work

  • A wooden or ceramic tray on each bedside surface — keeps things grouped and intentional
  • Dried botanicals (pampas grass, dried seed heads, eucalyptus) in a simple ceramic vase
  • A smooth river stone or piece of natural driftwood as a small sculptural object
  • A single scented or unscented candle in a ceramic holder
  • A woven or macramé textile hanging instead of framed art
  • A low floor cushion in natural linen near the window
  • A wooden magazine rack or single basket for bedside reading

Modern Japandi Bedroom Home Decor: Pulling It All Together

Modern Japandi bedroom home decor works by applying the Japandi philosophy with a slightly sharper, more contemporary eye. The warmth and natural materials are still there, but the forms are slightly cleaner and more geometric. If classic Japandi can feel very organic and handmade, modern Japandi has a crisper quality to it — a little more intentional in its geometry.

The way to pull it all together is through a clear visual hierarchy. The bed is the anchor. Bedside elements are the supporting cast. Wall decor is the punctuation — not the headline. Everything points back to that central sense of calm.

Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A modern Japandi bedroom with crisp warm white walls, a low platform bed in pale ash with clean geometric lines, two matching small square wooden bedside tables, a ceramic pendant light, a jute rug with a simple woven border, and a single trailing plant on a floating shelf. Everything feels intentional and clean. A South Asian couple — man and woman in their late thirties — are sitting on the edge of the bed, the woman leaning towards the man in easy relaxed conversation, natural and warm.]]

Modern Japandi decor checklist

  • Choose furniture with clean geometric forms — no curves, no ornate legs
  • Use matching or very closely tonal bedside pieces — asymmetry is less important here
  • Keep a consistent wood tone throughout the room — one species, one finish
  • Add one or two modern ceramic accent pieces in simple forms
  • Use a single oversized piece of modern Japandi wall art above the bed
  • Keep the rug simple — a low pile, solid or very subtly textured, in a tonal neutral

Small Japandi Bedroom Home Decor: Making It Work in Tight Spaces

Small Japandi bedroom home decor is, in many ways, easier than decorating a large room — the style's guiding principle of "less is more" is naturally suited to small spaces. The discipline of Japandi forces you to make exactly the decisions a small room demands: fewer pieces, more considered placement, and no visual clutter.

The biggest mistake in a small bedroom is trying to fill every surface and wall. A small Japandi bedroom should feel larger than its square footage because of what isn't there, not what is.

A small but beautifully styled Japandi bedroom: a low platform single or small double bed in pale oak, a wall-mounted bedside shelf (no floor table), a slim hanging mirror, a trailing plant on a wall bracket, and a small woven rug. A young white British woman in her mid-twenties is sitting cross-legged on the bed with a paperback book, completely relaxed and at home.]]

Small Japandi bedroom decor tips

  • Go low with furniture — a low bed makes ceilings feel higher
  • Use wall-mounted bedside shelves instead of floor-standing tables — frees up floorspace
  • A large mirror on one wall (simple, in natural wood) will make the room feel significantly bigger
  • Choose one piece of wall art — large format, not a gallery wall
  • A single small plant is enough — don't overcrowd the room with greenery
  • Use under-bed storage in proper fitted drawers to avoid a cluttered underside
  • Keep the rug smaller than the bed — it frames rather than dominates
Real Example: I once styled a box room in a Victorian terrace — just about large enough for a small double bed and a slim wardrobe. We went fully Japandi: everything was mounted to the wall (bedside shelf, lamp, art), we used a floor-to-ceiling mirror on the chimney breast, and chose a single trailing pothos on a wall bracket above the headboard. The client said it felt twice the size it had before. The secret was that we made the floor completely visible from the door.

DIY Japandi Bedroom on a Budget

You genuinely don't need a large budget to create a convincing Japandi bedroom. The philosophy actively works in your favour here — because restraint is built into the style, you're doing less rather than more. The money you save by not buying unnecessary things can go towards one or two quality pieces that really matter.

The key is to work in a clear order: declutter first, paint second (the single highest-impact change you can make for minimal cost), then address textiles, then lighting, then art and accessories. Don't skip to the fun parts before you've done the foundational work.

Warm afternoon light. A white British man in his early thirties is hanging a macramé wall textile, standing on a small step, focus and care visible in his posture.]]

Budget Japandi bedroom steps

  • Step 1 — Declutter: Remove everything from the room, then only bring back what genuinely belongs
  • Step 2 — Paint: One tin of warm white or greige paint transforms walls and woodwork together
  • Step 3 — Bedding: Replace synthetic bedding with affordable stonewashed linen or cotton — charity shops and sales are great sources
  • Step 4 — Lighting: Replace a harsh bulb with a warm-toned one, add a simple bedside lamp
  • Step 5 — DIY shelf: A simple wooden floating shelf (easy to fit yourself) adds architectural interest for minimal cost
  • Step 6 — Wall art: One well-chosen, well-framed print — doesn't need to be expensive, needs to be right
  • Step 7 — Plants: One or two easy, low-maintenance plants (more on this below)
Pro Tip: Paint is always the best-value single change you can make in any room. A tin of warm white matte paint applied to both the walls and the ceiling together makes a room feel simultaneously brighter and cosier — and it costs a fraction of new furniture.

Japandi Bedroom vs Scandinavian vs Wabi-Sabi — Key Differences

People often confuse these three styles because they share significant common ground. All three value simplicity and natural materials. But they come from different cultural roots and have meaningfully different priorities — understanding the differences helps you make sharper, more intentional choices.

The easiest way I explain it to clients: Scandinavian design optimises for function and social warmth. Wabi-sabi optimises for acceptance of imperfection and transience. Japandi sits in the middle — it takes Scandinavian livability and injects the Japanese reverence for imperfect beauty and restraint.

How to Transition an Existing Bedroom to Japandi Style Without a Full Renovation

This is the question I get asked most often, and my honest answer is: you can get 80% of the way to a Japandi bedroom without spending more than a few hundred pounds and without touching a single structural element. The transformation is in the editing, not the building.

The process works in phases. You don't need to do everything at once — in fact, it's better not to. Making one or two changes, living with them, and then deciding what to do next is exactly the kind of thoughtful, unhurried approach that the Japandi philosophy embodies.

Phase-by-phase transition plan

  • Phase 1 — Edit: Remove everything that doesn't serve rest or calm — decorative clutter, mismatched items, anything you've been meaning to throw away
  • Phase 2 — Paint: Paint the walls (and ceiling) in a warm white, greige, or muted sage — this single step does more than anything else
  • Phase 3 — Bedding: Swap synthetic bedding for linen or stonewashed cotton in warm neutrals
  • Phase 4 — Lighting: Change to warm-toned bulbs throughout, add a simple bedside lamp, dim or replace the ceiling light
  • Phase 5 — Wall art: Replace busy or mismatched art with one or two considered pieces in a Japandi style — or temporarily remove all art and live with just the wall for a week to understand what the space really needs
  • Phase 6 — Accessories: Introduce natural materials — a ceramic vase, dried botanicals, a wooden tray — and remove anything plastic or synthetic from visible surfaces
  • Phase 7 — Plants: Add one or two considered plants (see below for the best choices)

Pro Tip: Before spending a single penny, spend one hour removing items from your bedroom. Put everything that isn't fixed furniture or essential bedding into a box in another room. Then sit in the room for twenty minutes. You'll be surprised how much calmer it already feels — and what you decide you actually want to bring back.

Best Plants for a Japandi Bedroom

Plants in a Japandi bedroom are deliberate and minimal — you're not going for a lush jungle corner. One or two plants, chosen for their calm, architectural quality, is the approach. The goal is to bring nature inside quietly, not to make a statement with greenery.

The best plants for Japandi spaces are those that have a clean, simple visual form: a single arching stem, a compact rosette shape, or a quietly trailing quality that works from a shelf or wall bracket. They should also be low-maintenance — the philosophy of Japandi is about ease and peace, not constant effort.

Best plants for a Japandi bedroom

  • Snake plant (Sansevieria): Architectural, upright, very low maintenance — perfect for a floor corner or low shelf
  • Pothos (Epipremnum aureum): Trailing, forgiving, beautiful from a wall bracket or shelf — excellent for smaller bedrooms
  • Peace lily (Spathiphyllum): Soft, elegant, reportedly good for air quality — suits a floor spot in a larger bedroom
  • ZZ plant (Zamioculcas zamiifolia): Deep green, glossy, slow-growing — survives low light and minimal watering
  • Bonsai: The most authentically Japanese choice — slow, meditative, beautiful on a wooden shelf
  • Dried botanicals: Not technically a plant, but dried pampas, eucalyptus, and seed heads are very Japandi and entirely maintenance-free

Pro Tip: Always choose pots in ceramic, unglazed terracotta, or stone-effect finishes. The pot is as important as the plant in a Japandi bedroom. A beautiful plant in a plastic nursery pot sitting directly on a shelf breaks the aesthetic completely.

What is Japandi Style and How Does It Apply to the Bedroom?

Japandi is a design philosophy that merges the best of two distinct cultural aesthetics: Japanese minimalism — rooted in wabi-sabi, the beauty of imperfection — and Scandinavian hygge, which values warmth, simplicity, and functional cosiness. Applied to the bedroom, it means creating a space that is stripped of anything unnecessary, yet never feels stark or unwelcoming.

The bedroom is actually the ideal room to try this style because its whole purpose is rest. Every decision — furniture, colour, light, art — should serve that goal. That's exactly what Japandi thinking demands.

Core principles at a glance

  • Less is more — every item earns its place
  • Natural materials only: wood, linen, cotton, ceramic, stone
  • Neutral, earthy tones with no bright accent colours
  • Functionality is never sacrificed for style
  • Imperfections (a knot in wood, a slight texture variation) are celebrated
  • Calm and intention over trend-chasing
Pro Tip: Before you buy a single thing for a Japandi bedroom, take everything out of the room mentally and ask: "Would I miss this if it wasn't here?" If the answer is no, it probably shouldn't be in the room at all.

What Does a Japandi Bedroom Look Like?

A Japandi bedroom looks calm, grounded, and quietly beautiful. The first thing you notice is the absence of clutter — surfaces are clear, there are no decorative objects fighting for attention, and the room has a sense of intentional space. The second thing you notice is the warmth: despite being minimal, it never feels cold.

Visually, expect to see a low wooden bed frame, layered linen bedding in warm neutrals, a few carefully chosen ceramics, natural fibre rugs, and wall art that is understated rather than bold. It's the kind of room that makes you breathe out slowly the moment you walk in.

Key visual characteristics

  • Low-to-the-ground furniture, especially the bed
  • Warm neutral walls — stone, warm white, greige, soft sage
  • Visible natural grain in wood furniture
  • Textural contrast: smooth ceramics against rough linen, for example
  • A handful of plants, never an overwhelming collection
  • Minimal wall art — usually one or two pieces, well positioned
  • No overhead fluorescent lighting; warm, low, layered light only
Real Example: I had a client in Leeds who kept describing her bedroom as "blah" — she couldn't put her finger on why. It turned out she had three different wood tones, four different shades of beige with no clear logic, and six small decorative items on her dresser that had nothing to do with each other. We removed everything, chose one warm wood tone, and kept just two objects on the dresser. The room felt completely transformed without buying a single new piece of furniture.

Japandi Bedroom Furniture and Layout Essentials

Japandi bedroom furniture is characterised by clean lines, natural materials, and a deliberately low profile. The bed is usually the centrepiece — a simple platform or slat frame in pale ash, oak, or walnut, sitting close to the floor. Bedside tables, if present at all, are small and simple: a solid wood block, a ceramic stool, or a wall-mounted shelf.

Layout matters just as much as the individual pieces. Leave generous space around the bed, avoid pushing every piece of furniture against a wall, and resist the temptation to fill every corner. The empty space is part of the design.

Essential Japandi bedroom furniture pieces

  • Bed frame: Low platform, solid or slatted, in pale oak, ash or walnut — no upholstered headboards with heavy nailhead trim
  • Bedside storage: One small side table or wall-mounted shelf per side — keep surfaces minimal
  • Dresser/chest of drawers: Simple, handleless or with ceramic pulls, in a natural wood finish
  • Wardrobe: Flush-door, floor-to-ceiling if possible — avoids visual clutter at the top
  • Seating: Optional — a single low stool or cushioned bench at the foot of the bed if the room allows

Pro Tip: If your existing bed frame is too bulky, try removing the legs if they unscrew, or swap the headboard for a simple padded panel in a neutral linen fabric. Sometimes a small change to the dominant piece shifts the whole room's feel.

Japandi Bedroom Colour Palette and Materials

The Japandi colour palette is intentionally narrow and grounded in nature. Think warm white, soft stone, greige, warm sand, and muted sage — occasionally punctuated by a deeper charcoal or dark espresso in a furniture piece or textural accent. There are no bright, saturated colours anywhere in a true Japandi bedroom.

Materials are equally important. The textures you use carry as much visual weight as the colours. Raw linen, unpolished stone, undyed cotton, pale natural wood with visible grain, and hand-thrown ceramic all belong here. Avoid shiny surfaces, metallic finishes, and synthetic materials wherever possible.

Colour and material dos and don'ts

  • ✓ Warm whites and off-whites (never brilliant white)
  • ✓ Stone, sand, greige, warm taupe
  • ✓ Muted sage, dusty moss, soft olive
  • ✓ One darker anchor tone — charcoal or dark espresso
  • ✗ Bright whites, cool greys, or icy blues
  • ✗ Saturated accent colours — no mustard, terracotta, or teal
  • ✗ High-gloss lacquer, chrome, polished silver finishes
  • ✗ Synthetic textiles — polyester velvet, faux fur, plastic blinds
Pro Tip: Paint the ceiling in the same colour as the walls, or just one shade lighter. It makes the room feel more cocoon-like and cohesive — a trick I've used in every Japandi bedroom I've styled.

Japandi Bedroom Textiles and Soft Furnishings

Textiles are where the Japandi bedroom gets its warmth. The look might be minimal, but it should never feel hard or clinical — and the right soft furnishings are what make the difference. Linen is the star material here: used for bedding, curtains, and even cushion covers, it has that naturally wrinkled, lived-in quality that fits perfectly.

Layer your bedding in similar tones rather than contrasting patterns. A linen duvet cover in warm oatmeal, a cotton waffle throw, and two or three pillows in complementary neutrals is all you need. Resist the urge to pile on cushions — two or three is the absolute maximum.

Textile checklist for a Japandi bedroom

  • Linen or stonewashed cotton duvet cover — warm neutral tones only
  • A single textural throw — waffle cotton, chunky knit, or bouclé in a tonal colour
  • Two to three linen or cotton pillowcases — no printed patterns
  • A natural fibre rug: jute, seagrass, or a low-pile wool rug in stone or sand
  • Linen or cotton curtains — floor length, unlined or lightly lined, in warm white or greige
  • A small floor cushion or zabuton if you have floor space — nods to the Japanese influence

Pro Tip: Buy your bedding and curtains from the same colour family, not necessarily the same brand. Holding swatches together in natural light before you buy is the single best thing you can do to avoid a mismatch.

Japandi Bedroom Storage and Decluttering Principles

Hidden storage is fundamental to Japandi. Every object left on display is a deliberate choice — if it's not beautiful or useful, it goes behind a door. This isn't about being cold or sterile; it's about giving the things you do keep room to breathe and be appreciated.

The decluttering approach here borrows from both Japanese concepts — the idea that objects should bring joy and have a clear purpose — and Scandinavian practicality. If a thing doesn't serve the bedroom's purpose (rest and calm), it shouldn't be in the bedroom.

Practical Japandi storage rules

  • Conceal everything you use but don't want to look at: cables, chargers, medication, books
  • Use baskets in natural materials (wicker, seagrass) for things that need to be accessible
  • Limit open shelving — if you have a shelf, it should hold three items maximum
  • Under-bed storage is fine as long as it's in proper boxes or drawers — not random bags
  • If your wardrobe doors are messy or mismatched, consider simple replacement panels in a neutral tone
  • Remove anything from bedside surfaces that isn't essential — one or two items only
Real Example: I once helped a client clear a bedroom in Manchester that had seventeen items on her bedside table. Seventeen. We kept three: a small lamp, a ceramic cup for water, and a single book. She messaged me a week later to say she was sleeping better. I genuinely believe the visual calm of a tidy surface affects how well your brain switches off at night.

Japandi Bedroom Lighting and Accents

Lighting in a Japandi bedroom should always feel warm, low, and layered. Harsh overhead lighting is the enemy of this style — if you have a central ceiling light, put it on a dimmer immediately and use it only when you need to find something. The real atmosphere comes from table lamps, floor lamps, and wall-mounted sconces, all using warm-toned bulbs.

Paper or washi pendant lights, wooden lamp bases, and rattan shades all sit beautifully within the Japandi aesthetic. Accent lighting — a small candle, a low plug-in lamp — adds warmth in the evenings without overwhelming the space.

Japandi lighting guide

  • Ceiling: A single paper or washi pendant on a dimmer — no spotlights, no downlighters if avoidable
  • Bedside: A simple wooden or ceramic-base table lamp with a linen shade
  • Wall: A wooden or rattan wall sconce for ambient accent light
  • Floor: An arching floor lamp in solid wood or matte black for a reading corner
  • Bulbs: Warm white always — 2700K to 3000K, never cool daylight
  • Candles: Unscented or very lightly scented, in ceramic or simple glass vessels
